meta.blurb: Mina marks one acorn in the forest soil, then spends a year watching it with her grandfather Tomas. Through snow, spring and storm, they learn how trees and fungi trade, and why scientists still argue about how far it goes.
meta.bible:
Mina: a curious girl of about ten who asks why about everything. Tomas: her grandfather, a retired forester, patient and kind. They walk through one old forest in every season of one year, from Autumn to Autumn. The forest has Oak, Beech and Pine trees and a Stream. Suzanne Simard: a real forest scientist whose research on Mycorrhizal networks and Mother trees is real, though how much it matters for a whole forest is still Debated. Bristlecone pine: lives more than four thousand years, the oldest nearly five thousand. Redwood: Coast redwood of California by the Pacific, the tallest over one hundred Metres. Key terms: Acorn, Seedling, Jay, Chlorophyll, Photosynthesis, Stomata, Xylem, Phloem, Sap, Bark, Rings, Canopy, Understorey, Evergreen, Catkins, Fungi, Fungus, Mycorrhizal, Phosphorus, Deadwood, Carbon, Oxygen, Springtails, Hub trees, Nurse log. Voice: wondering, clear and kind. The science is real and hedged where scientists disagree: no invented numbers, studies or quotes. More key terms: Lichen, Lichens, Alga, Larch, Woodpecker, Dormouse, Mycorrhiza, Truffle, Truffles, Bumblebee, Ladybird. Charles Darwin: real naturalist who studied earthworms. Douglas fir: forest tree of western Canada where Suzanne Simard worked. Tomas's cottage stands at the forest edge. The stump on the path has sixty-one rings. Tomas's boyhood letter T is carved on a Beech.
More key terms: Caterpillar, Caterpillars.
More key terms: Mayflies, Caddisflies, Dipper, Glow-worms.
Van Helmont: a Flemish scientist of about four hundred years ago whose willow-in-a-pot experiment is real. Honey fungus in Oregon covers about nine square kilometres. The big Beech falls in the summer storm and opens a gap of light beside Mina's seedling. Mina's notebook has three columns: known, probable, still unknown. Dutch elm disease and ash dieback are real fungal diseases of trees.

beats.scene: Mina and her grandfather Tomas walk into a golden autumn forest at dawn
beats.summary: On an autumn morning, Mina and her grandfather Tomas begin a year of walking through the forest.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas cross a stream on flat stepping stones in morning mist
beats.summary: Tomas tells Mina that an old forest has its own rules, and that the first is to go slowly.

beats.scene: Mina stretches her arms but cannot reach around the huge old oak trunk
beats.summary: They reach a very old oak, and Tomas guesses that it has stood for over two hundred years.

beats.scene: Brown acorns fall like raindrops through yellow leaves onto the forest floor
beats.summary: In autumn the oak lets its acorns fall, and some years it drops far more than in others.

beats.scene: Tomas holds two halves of a split acorn in his open palm
beats.summary: Tomas opens an acorn to show that it is a seed, with a tiny tree and a store of food.

beats.scene: A squirrel, a deer and a mouse each search the leaves for acorns
beats.summary: Many animals eat acorns, so most of them will never become trees.

beats.scene: A jay carries an acorn in its beak between tall tree trunks
beats.summary: A jay buries acorns for winter, and it often carries them a long way from the oak.

beats.scene: A jay pushes an acorn into the soil while another waits on a branch
beats.summary: A jay forgets some of the acorns it hides, so forgetful birds help to plant forests.

beats.scene: Mina kneels by an acorn in damp soil and pushes a stick beside it
beats.summary: Mina finds one acorn already sinking into the soil and marks the spot with a stick.

beats.scene: Mina writes in a small notebook while Tomas smiles beside her
beats.summary: Mina writes the first line in her notebook, and Tomas asks what the acorn will be by next autumn.

beats.scene: Mina holds a yellow leaf against red and orange trees
beats.summary: Mina holds up a yellow leaf and asks why leaves change colour in autumn.

beats.scene: Sunlight glows through a bright green leaf held up in Mina's fingers
beats.summary: Tomas explains that leaves are green because of chlorophyll, which catches sunlight.

beats.scene: A tree with half green and half yellow leaves in cool morning light
beats.summary: Shorter days and cool nights make the tree stop making chlorophyll, so the green fades.

beats.scene: A pale yellow leaf and a golden orange leaf lie side by side
beats.summary: Yellow and orange were in the leaf all summer, hidden behind the green.

beats.scene: A blazing red maple leaf is held beside a plain brown oak leaf
beats.summary: Red is made fresh in autumn in some trees, and scientists still debate why.

beats.scene: Mina sorts fallen leaves into brown, copper, gold and red piles
beats.summary: Oak leaves turn brown, beech leaves turn copper, and each kind has its own colour.

beats.scene: Tomas holds a half yellow leaf up to the light while Mina looks
beats.summary: Before a leaf falls, the tree takes back valuable materials from it.

beats.scene: A leaf drops from its twig, leaving a small neat scar behind
beats.summary: The tree seals the base of each leaf, and the leaf lets go and falls.

beats.scene: Snow-laden branches bend beside bare ones in a cold forest
beats.summary: Dropping leaves helps a tree survive when water is frozen and snow is heavy.

beats.scene: Mina kicks through deep rustling leaves and presses one in her notebook
beats.summary: Mina presses an oak leaf and a beech leaf in her notebook as Tomas mentions the pines.

beats.scene: Mina lifts damp leaves and finds worms and tiny beetles beneath
beats.summary: Under the fallen leaves, Mina finds worms and beetles hard at work.

beats.scene: A fat earthworm pulls a brown leaf into a small hole in the soil
beats.summary: Earthworms drag leaves down into their burrows and mix them with the soil.

beats.scene: Tiny springtails and a woodlouse crawl over a torn brown leaf
beats.summary: Springtails, mites and woodlice chew leaves into crumbs.

beats.scene: White fungal threads spread across a rotting leaf like fine cobwebs
beats.summary: Fungi spread through the leaves and break them down.

beats.scene: Mina holds a handful of dark soil close to her eyes
beats.summary: Bacteria too small to see do much of the work, and a spoonful of soil holds billions.

beats.scene: Three leaves side by side show different stages of rotting
beats.summary: Over a year or more, a fallen leaf slowly turns into dark, crumbly soil.

beats.scene: Tomas points from a heap of rotting leaves up to the great oak
beats.summary: The nutrients return to the soil, and the roots of the trees take them up again.

beats.scene: Mina crouches and breathes in the smell of damp, dark soil
beats.summary: The smell of the forest comes partly from chemicals made by soil bacteria.

beats.scene: A small brown mushroom pushes up through the wet leaves
beats.summary: A mushroom is only the fruit of a fungus that lives mostly underground.

beats.scene: Mina tucks a blanket of leaves back over her marked acorn
beats.summary: Mina covers her acorn with leaves again, because a leaf blanket protects the ground.

beats.scene: Tomas points up through treetops, small trees and ferns below
beats.summary: Tomas describes the three main layers of a forest: canopy, understorey and floor.

beats.scene: Sunlit treetops spread like a green roof above a dim forest
beats.summary: The canopy is the roof of the forest, where the tallest trees catch the most sunlight.

beats.scene: Hazel, holly and young trees grow in the shade below the canopy
beats.summary: The understorey is made of smaller trees and shrubs that live in the shade.

beats.scene: Ferns and moss on a dim forest floor with one beam of light
beats.summary: Very little light reaches the forest floor, so only some plants can live there.

beats.scene: Mina looks up at a round hole high in the oak trunk
beats.summary: Different animals live at different heights, from owls in tree holes to beetles in the soil.

beats.scene: Tall beech trunks lean toward a gap in the leafy roof
beats.summary: Trees compete for light, and in crowded woods they grow tall and straight.

beats.scene: Mina touches a smooth grey beech trunk and then a rough ridged oak
beats.summary: Bark works like skin, protecting the living wood from cold, insects and even fire.

beats.scene: Tomas holds a strip of bark and points to the thin layer beneath it
beats.summary: Just under the bark, a thin living layer makes new wood and new bark each year.

beats.scene: Green moss and pale lichen cover patches of a trunk
beats.summary: Lichens are partnerships of fungus and alga, and moss grows wherever it is damp.

beats.scene: Mina leans with her cheek against the oak and looks up the trunk
beats.summary: Most of a trunk is dead wood, and only a thin outer layer is alive.

beats.scene: Mina counts the rings on a fresh stump with her fingertip
beats.summary: Mina counts sixty-one rings on a freshly cut stump beside the path.

beats.scene: Close view of one pale wide band and one dark thin band of wood
beats.summary: Each ring is a pale band of spring wood followed by a dark band of summer wood.

beats.scene: Mina touches the very centre ring of the stump while Tomas thinks
beats.summary: The oldest ring at the centre began when Tomas was a schoolboy.

beats.scene: Tomas points to wide and narrow rings as Mina leans close
beats.summary: Wide rings usually mean good years and narrow rings mean hard years, so rings record the weather.

beats.scene: A scientist's slice of wood beside an old beam from a church roof
beats.summary: Scientists match ring patterns from many trees to find the age of old timber.

beats.scene: A very narrow ring marked on a slice of wood by Mina's pencil
beats.summary: Rings hold clues to droughts and to cold summers after big volcanic eruptions.

beats.scene: A tree trunk grown over a rusty nail and an old branch scar
beats.summary: Trees grow over wounds, and the scars stay in the wood.

beats.scene: A split log with a dark centre and a pale outer ring
beats.summary: The dark heartwood in the middle is dead, and the pale sapwood outside carries water.

beats.scene: A beech trunk with a letter T cut into the smooth grey bark
beats.summary: Tomas shows an old carving at the same height it had when he was a boy.

beats.scene: The first frost whitens the leaves while Mina writes in her notebook
beats.summary: The first frost arrives, and Tomas says that the forest is about to rest.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas in wool hats walk through snow between bare trunks
beats.summary: Snow falls on the forest, and Mina and Tomas walk through the silent winter wood.

beats.scene: Mina scratches a bare twig with her thumbnail and finds green beneath
beats.summary: A bare tree is not dead, because a scratched twig still shows green under the bark.

beats.scene: Snow lies on dark green pine branches as Mina looks up
beats.summary: Pine trees keep their narrow, waxy needles all winter, so they are called evergreens.

beats.scene: Snow slides from a drooping pine branch in a soft white cloud
beats.summary: An evergreen's shape and flexible branches help it shed heavy snow.

beats.scene: A golden larch stands among dark pines with its needles falling
beats.summary: The larch is a cone-bearing tree that drops its needles in winter.

beats.scene: Two trees side by side, one bare and one green, in falling snow
beats.summary: Evergreen and leaf-dropping trees use two different ways of surviving the winter.

beats.scene: Tomas bends a snowy twig to show Mina its tight brown buds
beats.summary: Buds already hold the folded leaves of next spring, wrapped in tough scales.

beats.scene: Frost glitters on bare branches while Mina breathes out a white cloud
beats.summary: Trees change the liquid in their cells so that freezing does not tear them.

beats.scene: A squirrel digs in deep snow while a deer nibbles a twig nearby
beats.summary: Animals live through winter, and squirrels forget nuts that may sprout.

beats.scene: Mina brushes snow from her marker stick above the buried acorn
beats.summary: Many seeds need a spell of cold before they sprout, so the acorn waits.

beats.scene: A woodpecker clings to a tall grey dead trunk full of holes
beats.summary: A woodpecker drums on a standing dead tree, which is full of holes.

beats.scene: Holes in a dead trunk hold a sleeping owl and a blue tit
beats.summary: Old woodpecker holes become homes for owls, bats, bees and small birds.

beats.scene: Mina peels a strip of dead bark showing tunnels like carved patterns
beats.summary: Beetle larvae tunnel under loose bark, and woodpeckers hunt them.

beats.scene: A pale shelf-shaped fungus juts from the side of a dead trunk
beats.summary: Shelf fungi are the fruit of fungi that slowly rot the dead wood.

beats.scene: A dead tree surrounded by tiny drawings of beetles, moths, birds and bats
beats.summary: Many forest species depend on dead wood, perhaps about a fifth of them.

beats.scene: Tomas leans on a fallen trunk, looking back along a tidy forest edge
beats.summary: Foresters once cleared dead trees away, but many now leave some standing.

beats.scene: A sleepy bumblebee queen rests under moss beside a ladybird in bark
beats.summary: Many insects spend the winter asleep under moss and bark.

beats.scene: A small brown dormouse sleeps curled in a nest of leaves
beats.summary: Some animals hibernate and live on stored fat, and they must never be disturbed.

beats.scene: Blue tits and a robin feed together in a bare winter hazel
beats.summary: Birds stay through winter by feeding in flocks and eating seeds and insects.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas drink hot soup in a warm kitchen with a notebook open
beats.summary: At home, Mina writes a list of things that look dead in winter but are not.

beats.scene: Tomas kneels in snow and shows Mina a root wrapped in pale threads
beats.summary: Tomas shows Mina pale fungal threads wrapped around a fine tree root.

beats.scene: A close view of a handful of soil laced with white threads
beats.summary: A fungus is mostly a network of fine threads, and a pinch of soil holds metres of them.

beats.scene: A Greek word written in the snow with a stick beside a root
beats.summary: The partnership between fungus and root has a name, mycorrhiza, meaning fungus root.

beats.scene: White fungal threads wrap an oak root in dark soil
beats.summary: Trees give sugar to the fungus, and the fungus gives water and minerals back.

beats.scene: A fine fungal thread beside a root hair, drawn large in the notebook
beats.summary: Fungal threads are thinner than roots, so they reach tiny spaces and water that roots cannot.

beats.scene: A tall tree, a fern and a flower, each with threads at its roots
beats.summary: Most land plants have fungal partners, and the partnership is more than four hundred million years old.

beats.scene: A dog sniffs the ground at an oak root beside a truffle
beats.summary: Truffles are the fruit of fungi that live on the roots of oak and hazel trees.

beats.scene: Pale threads link the roots of several trees underground
beats.summary: Fungal threads can join several trees, and scientists have measured substances moving between them.

beats.scene: A tangle of glowing lines joins tree roots like a computer network
beats.summary: Journalists called this tangle the wood wide web, though it is only a comparison.

beats.scene: Mina frowns at her notebook beside Tomas, who raises one finger
beats.summary: Tomas warns Mina that the word talk may promise more than scientists know.

beats.scene: Mina looks up at the oldest oak with small seedlings at its base
beats.summary: Tomas tells Mina about old hub trees, and Suzanne Simard, who studied them in Canada.

beats.scene: A scientist holds a root tip beside a map of linked trees
beats.summary: Scientists used the DNA of fungi on roots to map which trees were linked underground.

beats.scene: Tiny seedlings in a dim spot are linked by threads to a tall tree
beats.summary: Some experiments suggest that seedlings linked to an old tree may grow better.

beats.scene: Fir seedlings in pots grow close to a bigger tree in a lab
beats.summary: One study hinted that a tree might favour its own seedlings, but more work is needed.

beats.scene: A stack of books and a paper with a question mark on a table
beats.summary: In 2023, scientists reviewed the research and said that some popular claims had too little evidence.

beats.scene: A fungus thread holds a drop of sugar while a tree root waits
beats.summary: The fungus might keep much of the sugar for itself, so nobody is sure who gains most.

beats.scene: A small pot with threads and roots beside a wide forest scene
beats.summary: Experiments in pots differ from real forests, so results are hard to carry over.

beats.scene: A scale with a tick on one side and a question mark
beats.summary: Fungi and their trade are real, but how much matters in a whole forest is still debated.

beats.scene: Mina writes in a notebook with three columns on a snowy log
beats.summary: Mina sorts the facts into known, probable and still unknown.

beats.scene: Tomas smiles at the snow-covered ground where the acorn lies hidden
beats.summary: Tomas says a good scientist is glad to say we do not know yet.

beats.scene: Soft rain falls on green buds as Mina and Tomas walk
beats.summary: The snow melts, soft rain falls, and the forest begins to wake.

beats.scene: Mina tastes a drop of clear sap from a cut birch twig
beats.summary: In spring, sap rises in trees, and people tap birch and maple trees for sweet sap.

beats.scene: Tomas and Mina watch small leaves burst from swollen buds on a branch
beats.summary: Buds swell and burst, and bright green leaves unfold.

beats.scene: A pale yellow butterfly rests on a primrose beside a fresh green fern
beats.summary: Birds, butterflies and flowers return as the days grow warmer and longer.

beats.scene: Mina crouches by the stick where a pale root leaves the acorn
beats.summary: Mina's acorn splits open, and a root pushes out first.

beats.scene: The two halves of an acorn cracked open around a pale young root
beats.summary: The root grows first, while the acorn's stored food feeds the seedling.

beats.scene: A turned jar shows a small root bending downward through damp paper
beats.summary: A root tip senses gravity, so roots grow downward however a seed lies.

beats.scene: A pale root covered in fine hairs grows down through dark soil
beats.summary: Root hairs take in water and minerals.

beats.scene: A white fungal thread touches the tip of a seedling's root
beats.summary: Fungal threads in the soil reach the young root, and a partnership may begin.

beats.scene: Mina measures the root with a ruler and draws it in her notebook
beats.summary: Mina measures the new root and draws it in her notebook.

beats.scene: Tomas draws wide spreading roots in the dust with a stick
beats.summary: Tomas draws the roots of the oak in the dust, wide and shallow, not deep like a carrot.

beats.scene: A thin root bends around a stone toward a patch of dark wet soil
beats.summary: Roots tend to grow toward wetter soil and to wind around stones.

beats.scene: A tree drawn with roots spread wider than its branches
beats.summary: Roots often spread wider than the branches, and most lie in the top layer of soil.

beats.scene: A young oak with one long root going straight down beside an older oak
beats.summary: A young oak grows a long taproot at first, and an old oak spreads wide.

beats.scene: A tree on a slope with roots gripping the soil and rocks
beats.summary: Roots hold the tree upright and also hold the soil in place.

beats.scene: Mina's boots press dark soil while a small root struggles for air
beats.summary: Roots need air as well as water, and soil that is trampled suffers.

beats.scene: A tiny green shoot rises from the soil beside the faded marker stick
beats.summary: A shoot rises from the acorn, and the seedling's first leaves unfold.

beats.scene: A small oak seedling stands at the edge of the old oak's shade
beats.summary: Seedlings in deep shade struggle, because oaks need light to grow.

beats.scene: A deer browses seedlings nearby while Mina's oak stands untouched
beats.summary: Animals eat many seedlings, and an oak needs only one of its acorns to succeed.

beats.scene: Mina holds a ruler beside the seedling and counts its small leaves
beats.summary: Mina measures her seedling and learns that it may have to wait a long time.

beats.scene: Fresh bright green leaves unfold on the oak as Mina looks up
beats.summary: The big oak opens its new leaves, which are soft and light green at first.

beats.scene: Sunlight shines through green oak leaves onto Mina's upturned face
beats.summary: Leaves catch sunlight with chlorophyll, which works like a tiny solar panel.

beats.scene: Arrows show sun, water and air entering a leaf, with sugar
beats.summary: Photosynthesis turns light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and releases oxygen.

beats.scene: A man in old clothes waters a small willow growing in a big pot
beats.summary: About four hundred years ago, van Helmont grew a willow in weighed soil for five years.

beats.scene: A scale shows a heavy willow tree beside a small pile of soil
beats.summary: The willow gained over seventy kilograms while the soil lost almost nothing.

beats.scene: A tall tree is drawn with air flowing into its leaves and trunk
beats.summary: A tree is built mostly from carbon taken from the air.

beats.scene: Ocean waves and a green forest side by side under a bright sun
beats.summary: Trees give out oxygen, but ocean algae make a large share of it too.

beats.scene: Mina sleeps while a tree at night uses sugar stored in its roots
beats.summary: A tree also uses its sugar for energy, and it stores some in its roots.

beats.scene: Mina studies the underside of a leaf with a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Tiny pores called stomata let gases in and out, and guard cells open and close them.

beats.scene: A hot dry afternoon, with wilting leaves and a tired Mina in the shade
beats.summary: On hot, dry days a tree closes its stomata to save water, and photosynthesis slows.

beats.scene: Tomas points up a tall trunk while Mina follows with her eyes
beats.summary: Water climbs from the roots to the highest leaves, and the tree has no heart to pump it.

beats.scene: A cut trunk shows a bundle of fine hollow tubes like drinking straws
beats.summary: Water travels through narrow tubes of wood called xylem.

beats.scene: A drop of water evaporates from a leaf and pulls a chain behind it
beats.summary: Water evaporating from the leaves pulls more water up behind it in an unbroken chain.

beats.scene: A very tall redwood drawn beside a house, a tower and a person
beats.summary: The tallest trees are over a hundred metres high, and calculations suggest a limit.

beats.scene: Mina stares at a bathtub and a row of buckets beside the oak
beats.summary: A big tree can lift hundreds of litres of water on a hot day.

beats.scene: Mina touches the bark of the oak while Tomas watches
beats.summary: Sugar travels down through the phloem, just under the bark.

beats.scene: A young tree with a ring of bark gnawed away around its trunk
beats.summary: If bark is stripped all the way around, sugar cannot reach the roots and the tree dies.

beats.scene: Tiny green aphids sit on a leaf while ants stroke them with their feelers
beats.summary: Aphids drink sugary sap, and the drops they let fall feed ants and bees.

beats.scene: Mina presses her ear to the oak trunk and listens carefully
beats.summary: Some scientists record tiny clicks from trees under drought, too faint for people to hear.

beats.scene: Mina draws water going up and sugar going down in a loop
beats.summary: Water goes up through the wood and sugar goes down through the bark, like a loop.

beats.scene: A blue tit carries moss to a nest hole in a trunk at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn the forest fills with birdsong, and a blue tit carries moss to its nest.

beats.scene: A blue tit parent brings a green caterpillar to hungry chicks in a hole
beats.summary: Blue tit chicks need thousands of caterpillars, so the birds time their nesting with the new leaves.

beats.scene: A calendar page with two arrows, one for leaves and one for caterpillars
beats.summary: Warm springs can change the timing of leaves and caterpillars, so birds may fall out of step.

beats.scene: Long yellow catkins hang from oak twigs beside tiny green flowers
beats.summary: The oak has hanging male flowers and tiny female flowers on the same tree.

beats.scene: A cloud of yellow pollen rises from a pine in the sunshine
beats.summary: Pollen drifts on the wind, and wind-pollinated trees make millions of grains.

beats.scene: Bees crowd on golden willow catkins and pink cherry blossom
beats.summary: Bees visit blossom and willow catkins, and trees that need insects use flowers and sweet nectar.

beats.scene: A forest floor covered with acorns in a heavy year beside a bare one
beats.summary: Oaks make a huge crop of acorns only in some years, and scientists still debate why.

beats.scene: Bluebells and white anemones carpet a sunny floor under bare branches
beats.summary: Spring flowers bloom on the forest floor before the leaves above them close the light.

beats.scene: A tawny owl chick sits fluffy on a branch near its nest hole
beats.summary: A tawny owl chick leaves its nest hole and sits on a branch to wait for food.

beats.scene: Mina measures her seedling with a ruler in the golden evening light
beats.summary: Mina's seedling now has six leaves, and the evenings are long and bright.

beats.scene: A green caterpillar chews a lacy hole in a young oak leaf
beats.summary: Caterpillars eat the young leaves, and the oak has ways to defend itself.

beats.scene: Tiny caterpillars hang on silk threads from an oak branch above Mina
beats.summary: Winter moth caterpillars lower themselves on silk threads, and one lands on Mina's hat.

beats.scene: A tender pale leaf beside a tough dark leaf with bitter tannin drops
beats.summary: Young leaves are soft and easy to eat, but older oak leaves are tough and bitter with tannins.

beats.scene: A chewed oak leaf with a small arrow pointing to nearby leaves
beats.summary: A chewed leaf sends a signal inside the tree, and other leaves make more defences.

beats.scene: Mina sniffs a torn leaf beside a neighbouring tree with green leaves
beats.summary: A torn leaf gives off the smell of cut grass, a mix of chemicals released by damage.

beats.scene: Two rows of young trees, one chewed and one untouched, share a hilltop
beats.summary: Some experiments suggested that neighbouring trees respond to these chemicals, but scientists still debate it.

beats.scene: A tiny wasp lands on a chewed leaf beside a caterpillar
beats.summary: The same chemicals may attract wasps and birds that attack the caterpillars.

beats.scene: Mina looks at a leafy oak village with tiny paths between the trees
beats.summary: Tomas says a tree is not making plans, because these responses were shaped by evolution.

beats.scene: A brown round oak apple growing on a twig beside a tiny wasp
beats.summary: Gall wasps lay eggs in oak buds, and the tree grows a round ball around each egg.

beats.scene: Mina writes a line of dark ink on paper with a feather pen
beats.summary: People made ink from oak galls for centuries and wrote famous documents with it.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas rest in deep green shade beside a sparkling stream
beats.summary: In midsummer, the forest is a cool green room, and the fields outside are hot.

beats.scene: A thermometer in the shade beside a thermometer in a sunny field
beats.summary: The forest is cooler because of shade and because leaves release water vapour, which cools the air.

beats.scene: Warm moist air rises from the forest canopy into a cloud above
beats.summary: Forests add water vapour to the air, and some scientists think this helps bring rain.

beats.scene: Rain falls on the canopy while Mina and Tomas stand dry underneath
beats.summary: The canopy catches rain, and the soil releases it slowly.

beats.scene: Mina lifts a flat stone in the stream and finds tiny creatures
beats.summary: Insects such as mayflies and caddisflies live in clean, cool stream water.

beats.scene: Brown leaves lie in the stream while a small larva chews one
beats.summary: Leaves that fall into the stream feed the creatures that live there.

beats.scene: A dipper stands on a wet stone while a trout rests in shade
beats.summary: Shade keeps the stream cool, and cool water helps trout and many other animals.

beats.scene: Bats flicker over the clearing at dusk against a pink sky
beats.summary: At dusk, bats leave their roosts in tree holes to hunt for insects.

beats.scene: Tiny green lights glow in the grass at the forest edge
beats.summary: Glow-worms glow in the grass to attract mates.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas lie on a blanket looking at stars between treetops
beats.summary: At night, trees stop making sugar, and a tree's branches may droop a little.

beats.scene: Dark clouds gather as Mina and Tomas run to a rocky overhang
beats.summary: A summer storm comes, and Mina and Tomas shelter under a rock as the wind bends the treetops.

beats.scene: A staked young tree beside a free tree swaying in the wind
beats.summary: Wind makes trees stronger, because swaying makes a trunk thicker.

beats.scene: A wide lone oak in a field beside tall thin forest trees
beats.summary: Trees in the open grow wide, while trees in a crowded wood grow tall and thin.

beats.scene: A flash of lightning behind a tall oak while Mina covers her ears
beats.summary: Lightning often strikes tall trees, and some survive with a long scar.

beats.scene: A huge beech lies on the ground, its roots lifted like a wall
beats.summary: After the storm, a giant beech lies on its side with its roots torn out of the ground.

beats.scene: Mina touches the wall of earth and roots standing on its edge
beats.summary: Beeches have shallow roots, so a storm on wet soil can topple even a very old tree.

beats.scene: A bright patch of sunlight falls on the floor beside Mina's seedling
beats.summary: The fallen tree has opened a gap of light, just beside Mina's seedling.

beats.scene: Birch and bramble seedlings crowd into a sunny gap in the forest
beats.summary: Fast-growing trees and plants rush into a gap, so the forest is a patchwork of ages.

beats.scene: Tomas touches a blackened pine trunk with green shoots at its base
beats.summary: An old fire scar on a pine shows that some trees can survive and recover.

beats.scene: Pine cones opening in the heat of a distant fire beside green seedlings
beats.summary: Some pines have cones that open in fire, but fire today often burns too hot and too often.

beats.scene: A mossy fallen log with ferns, mushrooms and small seedlings on top
beats.summary: Months later, the fallen beech is covered in moss, ferns and mushrooms.

beats.scene: A fat beetle grub inside a soft, rotten log beside a stag beetle
beats.summary: Beetles and their grubs live in rotting wood, and some take years to grow up.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass over a log with white and brown streaks of rot
beats.summary: Wood is hard to digest, and fungi that rot it are among the few that can.

beats.scene: A row of small trees growing in a line along an old mossy log
beats.summary: Seedlings often sprout along a rotting log, which is called a nurse log.

beats.scene: A log shrinking over the years beside a thread of dark soil
beats.summary: The carbon in a fallen tree returns slowly to the air and soil as it rots.

beats.scene: Tomas gently pushes Mina's hand away from a pale mushroom
beats.summary: Tomas warns Mina never to eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has named it.

beats.scene: A huge map with a single fungus coloured across a whole forest
beats.summary: A honey fungus in Oregon covers about nine square kilometres, and may be thousands of years old.

beats.scene: A yellow-brown mushroom cluster at the base of a sick young tree
beats.summary: Not all fungi are friends, and honey fungus can kill living trees.

beats.scene: A bare elm tree beside a beetle on peeling bark
beats.summary: Dutch elm disease, spread by beetles, killed millions of elm trees in the last century.

beats.scene: Mina writes in her notebook beside a bare ash tree in the fog
beats.summary: Diseases now travel the world with trade, but scientists look for resistant trees.

beats.scene: Tomas opens a book showing a twisted ancient pine on a dry mountain
beats.summary: On a rainy evening, Tomas shows Mina a book about the oldest trees in the world.

beats.scene: A twisted bristlecone pine clings to a rocky white mountainside
beats.summary: Bristlecone pines grow high in the dry mountains of the western United States, and some are almost five thousand years old.

beats.scene: A bristlecone trunk is mostly bare dead wood with one strip of green
beats.summary: Slow growth and dense resinous wood help bristlecone pines resist rot and live for thousands of years.

beats.scene: Scientists match rings from a living pine with those of old dead wood
beats.summary: Scientists matched living and dead bristlecone wood to build a ring record that goes back thousands of years.

beats.scene: Giant redwoods in morning fog tower over tiny walkers below
beats.summary: Tomas tells Mina about the coast redwoods, which are the tallest trees, over a hundred metres high.

beats.scene: Redwood roots joined underground while a salamander climbs high in the canopy
beats.summary: Redwood roots join those of their neighbours, and soil and small animals live high in their crowns.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas walk through falling gold leaves toward the oak
beats.summary: Autumn returns, and Mina and Tomas walk again to the old oak.

beats.scene: Mina kneels beside a small oak seedling and the old grey stick
beats.summary: Mina finds her seedling alive beside the faded stick, a year older.

beats.scene: A small seedling in a pool of light beside a fallen beech
beats.summary: The seedling is still small, but the gap has given it light, and it will wait for many years.

beats.scene: A tiny redwood seed, a bristlecone seed and an acorn lie on Mina's palm
beats.summary: Every giant began as a small seed, and Mina's oak is only at the beginning.

beats.scene: Mina presses her hands to a trunk while sunlight warms the leaves
beats.summary: Trees store carbon in their wood, roots and soil, and forests matter for the climate.

beats.scene: A burning forest releases smoke beside a wide green wood standing calm
beats.summary: Burned or cleared forests give their carbon back to the air, so keeping old forests helps.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas watch a deer drink at a clear forest stream
beats.summary: Forests also shelter animals, hold soil in place and keep water clean.

beats.scene: A map of a green forest, a golden meadow and a dark peat bog
beats.summary: Planting trees helps when the right kinds go in the right places, but not everywhere.

beats.scene: A very old oak beside a tiny young tree and a root map
beats.summary: Old forests have soil, fungi and ancient trees that no planting can quickly replace.

beats.scene: Mina and neighbours plant a young tree in a sunny field
beats.summary: Mina and her neighbours plant a young tree on a village planting day.

beats.scene: Mina steps carefully along a narrow path past a fallen branch
beats.summary: Tomas gives two rules: leave deadwood where it lies, and walk lightly.

beats.scene: Mina reads through her full notebook beside a window and a candle
beats.summary: Mina reads her notebook and sees how many questions have become answers.

beats.scene: Mina picks up a good acorn from the path in the golden light
beats.summary: Mina chooses a good acorn on the path and decides to plant it.

beats.scene: Mina presses an acorn into the earth while Tomas smiles beside her
beats.summary: Mina plants her own acorn, joining the long work of the forest.

A1A2: Mina and her grandfather Tomas walk into the forest on an autumn morning.
They cross the stream on flat stones, and the air is full of mist.
The oak is so wide that Mina cannot reach around it.
The old oak drops its acorns, and they fall like small brown rain.
Tomas cuts an acorn open, and inside it there is a little tree.
Squirrels, deer and mice all come to the forest to eat acorns.
A jay picks up an acorn and flies away with it.
The jay hides the acorn in the soil, but it forgets some.
Mina finds one acorn in the wet soil and puts a stick beside it.
Mina writes about the acorn in her notebook, and Tomas smiles at her.
Mina holds up a yellow leaf and asks why the leaves change.
Leaves are green because of chlorophyll, and chlorophyll catches the light from the sun.
In autumn the days get short and cold, and the green goes away.
The yellow and orange were in the leaf all summer, but green hid them.
Some trees make new red colour in autumn, and nobody knows exactly why.
Oak leaves turn brown, beech leaves turn copper, and some maples turn red.
The tree takes back the good things from each leaf before it falls.
At the end of the leaf stalk, the tree closes a small door.
Without leaves, the tree loses less water, and snow cannot weigh it down.
Mina walks through the dry leaves, and they make a loud noise.
Under the leaves, Mina finds worms and tiny beetles.
A worm pulls a leaf into the ground and eats it.
Tiny animals chew the leaves into very small pieces.
White threads grow through the leaves and make them soft.
One spoon of soil holds billions of tiny living things.
After many months, an old leaf becomes dark, soft soil.
The trees take the good things back up through their roots.
Mina smells the soil, and it smells like the forest.
A small mushroom grows up through the wet leaves.
Mina puts the leaves back over her acorn, like a blanket.
Tomas shows Mina three parts of the forest: high, middle and low.
The tall trees make a green roof, and they get the most sun.
Under the roof, smaller trees and bushes grow in the shade.
Only a little light reaches the ground, so only some plants grow there.
Mina sees a round hole high in the oak, where an owl sleeps.
The trees race upward to find the light, and they grow tall and straight.
The bark of a tree is like skin, and it keeps the tree safe.
Under the bark is a thin living layer that makes new wood.
Moss and lichen grow all over the bark wherever it is wet.
Most of the trunk is dead wood, and only the outside is alive.
Mina counts the rings on a new stump, and she finds sixty-one.
Each ring has a wide pale part and a thin dark part.
The middle ring began when Tomas was a boy at school.
Wide rings show good years, and thin rings show hard years.
Scientists compare rings from many trees to find the age of old wood.
Some rings show a dry year or a very cold summer.
When a tree is hurt, new wood grows over the wound.
The middle of the trunk is dark, and the outside is pale.
Tomas cut a letter in a beech tree when he was a boy.
The first frost comes, and the leaves turn white in the morning.
Snow falls on the forest, and the whole wood is very quiet.
Mina scratches a branch, and under the bark she sees green.
Pine trees keep their thin needles all winter, so they stay green.
The pine branches bend, and the snow slides off in soft clouds.
The larch tree is different, because it drops its needles in winter.
Some trees keep their leaves, and others drop them, and both can work.
On every bare branch, small buds hold the leaves for next spring.
Even in the frost, the trees change themselves, and the ice does no harm.
A squirrel digs in the snow for nuts that it hid.
Mina brushes the snow off her stick and thinks about the acorn below.
A woodpecker taps on a dead tree, and the wood has many holes.
Owls, bats and small birds live in the old holes.
Under the loose bark, small beetles make tunnels in the wood.
A pale fungus grows out of the dead trunk like a shelf.
Many forest animals and plants need dead wood to live.
Years ago, workers cleared the dead trees, but now some stay.
Many insects sleep through the winter under moss and bark.
A small dormouse sleeps in a nest, and Mina does not wake it.
Small birds stay together in winter and look for food in groups.
At home, Mina drinks hot soup and writes a new list.
Tomas brushes away the snow and shows Mina white threads around a root.
Fungus is mostly made of thin threads, and the soil is full of them.
The partnership between fungus and root has a long name: mycorrhiza.
The tree gives sugar to the fungus, and the fungus gives water back.
The fungus threads are thinner than roots, so they reach more water.
Most land plants have fungus partners, and this is very old.
A truffle is a fungus that grows under the ground near oak roots.
One fungus can join the roots of many trees in the ground.
Some people call this the wood wide web, like the internet.
Tomas says the word talk might say too much about the trees.
Tomas tells Mina about hub trees and a scientist named Suzanne Simard.
Scientists used fungus DNA to find which trees were joined underground.
Some small trees linked to old trees seem to grow better.
One study hints that a tree may help its own young trees.
In 2023, scientists said that some claims have too little proof.
Maybe the fungus keeps most of the sugar for itself.
It is hard to test this, because the forest is so big.
The fungi are real, but we do not know their full job.
Mina writes three headings in her notebook: known, probable and unknown.
Tomas smiles and says, we do not know yet, and that is fine.
The snow melts, the rain is soft, and the forest begins to wake.
Sap rises in the trees, and people take a little from birch trees.
Small buds swell and burst, and bright green leaves open.
The days get warm and long, and birds and butterflies come back.
Mina's acorn has split open, and a pale root comes out.
The acorn's food feeds the young plant while the root grows.
Roots always grow downward, even when a seed lies on its side.
The root has very fine hairs, and they drink water from the soil.
A fungus thread touches the new root, and a partnership may begin.
Mina measures the root with a ruler and draws it carefully.
Tomas draws roots in the dust, and they spread wide, not deep.
Roots grow toward wet soil, and they go around stones.
Roots often spread wider than the branches, and most are near the top.
A young oak grows one long root down, and an old oak spreads wide.
Roots hold the tree up, and they also hold the soil.
Roots need air, so heavy feet can hurt the soil.
A small green shoot comes up beside Mina's old stick.
The little oak stands in the shade, but oaks need a lot of light.
Animals eat many small trees, but Mina's oak is lucky.
Mina measures her little oak and counts its first small leaves.
The big oak opens its new leaves, which are soft and light green.
The leaves catch the light from the sun and use it.
The leaf takes in light, water and air, and it makes sugar.
Long ago, a man weighed a small tree and the soil it grew in.
The tree got heavier, but the soil weighed almost the same.
The wood is mostly made from air, and that surprises Mina.
Trees give out oxygen, but the sea plants make a lot too.
The tree uses some sugar for energy, and it keeps some in the roots.
Tiny holes in the leaf let air in and let water out.
On hot days, the tree closes its tiny holes to save water.
Water climbs up the trunk from the roots to the leaves.
The water goes through very thin tubes in the wood.
Water leaves the leaf, and that pulls more water up the tree.
The tallest trees are over a hundred metres high.
On a hot day, a big tree can lift hundreds of litres of water.
Sugar from the leaves travels down just under the bark.
If the bark is cut all the way around, the tree dies.
Tiny green insects drink the sweet sap, and ants come to eat it.
Mina puts her ear on the oak, but she hears nothing.
Water goes up inside the wood, and sugar comes down under the bark.
At dawn, birds sing, and a blue tit carries moss to its nest.
The baby birds eat thousands of green caterpillars before they leave.
In a warm spring, leaves and caterpillars may come too early for the birds.
The oak has long yellow flowers that hang down, and tiny flowers beside them.
The wind carries the yellow pollen from tree to tree.
Bees visit the blossom and the willow flowers to find sweet food.
Some years the oak makes a huge number of acorns, and some years almost none.
Spring flowers bloom on the ground before the leaves above close out the light.
A young owl sits on a branch and waits for its parents.
Mina's little oak now has six leaves, and the evening is bright.
A green caterpillar chews a hole in a young oak leaf.
Tiny caterpillars hang from the branch on silk threads, and one lands on Mina.
Young leaves are soft, but old oak leaves are tough and bitter.
A chewed leaf sends a signal, and the other leaves get ready.
A torn leaf smells like cut grass, and the smell is a message.
Maybe nearby trees notice the smell, but scientists do not agree.
The smell can bring a wasp, and the wasp attacks the caterpillar.
Tomas says that the tree does not plan, because evolution shaped these changes.
A small wasp lays an egg in a bud, and a ball grows.
People used to make ink from these oak balls.
In the middle of summer, the forest is cool, and the fields outside are hot.
Shade and wet leaves make the forest cooler than the fields.
Forests send water into the air, and this may bring rain.
The leaves catch the rain, and the water reaches the ground slowly.
In the cold stream, Mina finds tiny animals under a flat stone.
Leaves fall into the stream, and small animals eat them.
The shade keeps the water cool, and the fish like it.
At dusk, the bats come out and catch insects in the air.
Small green lights shine in the grass at the edge of the forest.
At night, trees stop making sugar, and Mina looks at the stars.
A summer storm comes, and Mina and Tomas hide under a big rock.
Wind shakes the trees, and the shaking makes the trunk stronger.
A tree in a field grows wide, but a forest tree grows tall.
Lightning flashes, and a tall oak is hit by the light.
After the storm, a huge beech tree lies on the ground.
The beech has shallow roots, and the wet ground could not hold it.
Now a hole in the roof lets sunlight fall near Mina's tree.
Fast young trees and bushes grow quickly into the sunny space.
Tomas shows Mina a black mark on an old pine from a fire.
Some pine cones open in a fire, but too much fire is bad.
Months later, the fallen beech is covered with moss and mushrooms.
Beetles and their young live in the soft rotten wood for years.
Wood is hard to eat, but some fungi can break it down.
Small trees grow in a line along the rotting log.
As the log rots, its carbon goes slowly back to the air and soil.
Tomas tells Mina never to eat a wild mushroom.
One honey fungus in the United States covers many square kilometres.
Some fungi are not friends, and they can kill trees.
Elm trees got a sickness, and millions of them died.
New tree diseases travel the world, but scientists look for strong trees.
On a rainy evening, Tomas shows Mina a book about very old trees.
Bristlecone pines grow on dry mountains, and some are almost five thousand years old.
They grow slowly, and their hard wood does not rot, so they live long.
Scientists compared old and living wood, and they read thousands of years of rings.
Redwoods are the tallest trees, and they are over a hundred metres high.
Redwood roots join together underground, and animals live high in the branches.
Autumn comes again, and Mina and Tomas walk through the gold leaves.
Mina finds her little oak alive beside the old stick.
Her little oak is still small, but now it gets some light.
Every giant tree began as a seed, and so did Mina's oak.
Trees store carbon in their wood, their roots and the soil.
When a forest burns, the carbon goes back into the air.
A deer drinks at the clear stream, and Mina tries not to move.
Planting trees helps, but only the right trees in the right places.
Old forests hold soil, fungi and ancient trees that are hard to replace.
Mina and her neighbours plant a young tree in a sunny field.
Walk on the paths and leave the fallen branches where they lie.
Mina reads her notebook and sees how much she has learned.
Mina finds a good acorn on the path and holds it carefully.
Mina plants an acorn at the edge of the forest and smiles.
B1B2: Mina has come to the old forest with her grandfather Tomas, who used to be a forester. He has promised to walk with her through every season of one whole year.
They cross the Stream on flat stepping stones while the mist is still lifting. Tomas tells her that an old forest has its own rules, and that the first rule is to go slowly.

At the end of the path they reach an oak so wide that Mina cannot put her arms around it. Tomas guesses that it has stood there for more than two hundred years, though nobody wrote down the day it began.
In autumn the oak lets go of its acorns, and they patter down through the yellow leaves like brown rain. Some years the tree drops a huge number of them, and in other years it drops hardly any.
Tomas finds a fresh acorn and opens it carefully with his pocket knife. Inside there is a tiny pale tree, packed in beside the food that will keep it alive until it finds light.
A squirrel rushes past, and a deer lifts its head to listen. Mice, pigeons and wild boar all eat acorns too, so most of the acorns that fall will never become trees.
A jay lands on a low branch and fills its throat with acorns, one after another. Then it flies away between the trunks, often carrying its load a long way from the oak.
The jay presses each acorn into the soil to save it for winter. It cannot remember every hiding place, so the acorns it forgets are given a chance to grow.
Mina finds one acorn half sunk in the damp soil, with its shell still shining. She pushes a stick in beside it, because she wants to watch what happens to it this year.

That evening Mina opens a new notebook and writes the date and the words one acorn. Tomas asks her what she thinks it will be by next autumn, and she cannot decide whether to say a tree or nothing at all.
Mina holds up a yellow leaf against a hillside of red and orange trees. She wants to know why a leaf that was green all summer changes colour in autumn.

Tomas tells her that leaves are green because they are full of chlorophyll, a substance that catches sunlight. A leaf uses that light to make food for the tree, and it needs a lot of chlorophyll to do it.
As the days grow shorter and the nights grow cooler, the tree stops making new chlorophyll. The old chlorophyll breaks down, and slowly the green fades out of the leaf.
Underneath the green, the leaf has held yellow and orange substances all summer long. They were only hidden, and now that the chlorophyll is gone, everyone can see them.
Red is different, because many trees make it fresh in the autumn. Scientists have several ideas about why, and so far none of them has been proved to everyone's satisfaction.
Mina starts to sort the fallen leaves into piles by colour. Oak leaves turn mostly brown, beech leaves glow copper, and a few maples near the Stream have turned a deep red.
Tomas shows her a leaf that is only half yellow. The tree does not simply throw its leaves away, he says, because it first draws back some of their valuable materials and stores them.

Where each leaf joins the twig, the tree builds a thin layer of new cells. When the layer is finished, the leaf comes away at the slightest breath of wind, and the tree is left with a neat, sealed scar.

A broad, thin leaf loses water into the air all the time, and in winter the roots cannot drink from frozen ground. Wet snow would also pile up on the leaves and break the branches, so dropping them is a clever way to survive.

Soon the whole floor of the forest is a thick, rustling carpet, and Mina enjoys every noisy step she takes. She presses an oak leaf and a beech leaf between the pages of her notebook, and Tomas says that pine trees do things very differently.

Mina lifts a layer of damp leaves with a stick and finds a hidden world beneath. Worms, beetles and tiny pale creatures are crawling through the dark, wet litter, and none of them seems to notice her.

An earthworm is pulling a leaf down into a narrow burrow, one small tug at a time. Tomas tells her that Charles Darwin studied worms for years, and that he wrote a whole book about how much soil they move.

Springtails, mites and woodlice are chewing the leaves into smaller and smaller pieces. A springtail is so tiny that Mina can only see it when it jumps, flicking itself into the air with a little spring.
White threads of fungus are spreading across the rotting leaves like fine cobwebs. The fungus makes chemicals that soften the leaf from outside, and then it soaks up the food that is set free.

Tomas scoops up a handful of soil and tells her that it is crowded with life too small to see. Bacteria do a great deal of the work of rotting, and a single spoonful of healthy soil can hold billions of them.

Mina compares three leaves from the path: one is almost whole, one is full of holes, and one is little more than brown lace. Tomas says that a leaf may take a year or more to turn into dark, crumbly soil, and that some kinds rot faster than others.

The leaves that fell last year are being turned back into the materials that trees need. Tomas points at the old oak and says its roots will take them up again, so the tree feeds on its own old leaves.

Mina kneels and breathes in the smell of the damp soil, which reminds her of rain on a dry path. Tomas says that part of this smell comes from a chemical made by soil bacteria, and that people can notice it in tiny amounts.

A small brown mushroom has pushed up through the wet leaves, and Mina bends to look at it. Tomas explains that a mushroom is only the fruit of a fungus, and that the rest of it lives hidden in the ground.

Mina checks her marker stick and sees that the wind has blown a few leaves away from the acorn. She tucks them back, and Tomas says that a blanket of leaves keeps frost out of the ground and holds water in.

Tomas points up through the treetops and shows Mina that a forest has layers, like a tall building. The highest layer is the canopy, the middle layer is the understorey, and the lowest is the forest floor.
The canopy is the roof of the forest, made of the crowns of the tallest trees. These trees catch most of the sunlight, and the leaves below must live on whatever light is left over.
Under the canopy grow smaller trees and shrubs, such as hazel, holly and hawthorn. Some of them will always be small, but others are young trees that are waiting for a chance to grow tall.

Down on the forest floor it is dim and quiet, and the air feels cool and damp. Only a small part of the sunlight reaches the ground, so only ferns, moss and a few special flowers can live in the shade.
High in the oak, Mina notices a round dark hole in the trunk where a branch once broke off. Tomas says that a tawny owl may sleep there by day, while beetles and worms live in the soil far below it.
Beech trunks lean slightly towards a gap in the leafy roof where the sun shines through. Trees in a crowded wood race for light, so they grow tall and straight with most of their leaves at the top.

Mina touches the smooth grey bark of a beech and then the deep ridges of the oak, and the two feel completely different. Tomas says that bark works like skin, because it protects the living wood from cold, insects and sometimes even fire.

Tomas picks up a loose strip of bark and shows her the damp, pale layer that lay beneath it. This thin layer is where the tree really grows, because it adds new wood on its inside and new bark on its outside every year.
Green moss and pale grey lichens are growing on the bark in patches. A lichen is a fungus and an alga living together, and moss grows wherever it is damp, so it is not a compass.

Mina rests her cheek against the oak and looks up along the trunk, which seems to go on for ever. Tomas says that most of a trunk is dead wood that holds the tree up, and only a thin outer layer is alive.

Beside the path lies a freshly cut stump, and Mina bends over it to count the rings with her fingertip. Tomas says the tree was leaning over the path and had to come down, and she reaches sixty-one before she stops.
When Mina looks closely, she sees that every ring has two parts. The pale part grew quickly in spring, and the darker, thinner part grew slowly in summer, so the two together make one year.
Mina rests her finger on the very centre of the stump. Tomas says that this ring was made when he was a schoolboy, and he is quiet, thinking about everything that has happened since.

Mina notices that the rings are not all the same width, and Tomas says that the trunk is a diary of the weather. In a wet, warm year a tree usually grows a wide ring, but in a dry or cold year the ring is thin.

Tomas explains that scientists compare the ring patterns of many trees, like a very long code. By matching old patterns with new ones, they can find the year in which a beam in an old church roof was cut.
Mina marks one very narrow ring with her pencil and asks what happened that year. Tomas says that it could have been a drought, or a cold summer after one of the great volcanic eruptions.
On a nearby beech, Mina finds a rusty nail that the trunk has grown right over. The tree cannot heal a wound the way skin does, so it closes it with new wood, and the scar stays inside for ever.
Tomas splits a log to show her the middle of a trunk. The dark core is heartwood, which is dead and holds the tree up, while the pale outer ring is sapwood, which carries water.

On a smooth grey beech, Mina finds a letter T that Tomas cut into the bark when he was a boy. She is surprised that it is still at the same height, but Tomas says that trees grow taller only from their tips.
One morning the grass crunches under their boots, and the last leaves are white with the first frost. Mina writes the date in her notebook, and Tomas says that the forest is about to rest.
Snow begins to fall in thick, soft flakes, and Mina and Tomas pull on their wool hats. The forest is white and silent, and their boots make the only sound as they walk between the bare trunks.
The trees look dead, but Tomas shows Mina a simple test. When she scratches a twig with her thumbnail, she finds a thin green layer under the bark, so the tree is only resting.
Pine trees are different from oaks, because they keep their needles all winter. The needles are narrow and covered with a waxy skin, so they lose very little water to the cold, dry air.

Snow lies heavily on a pine branch until the branch bends and tips it off in a soft white cloud. Tomas says that the shape of many evergreens, with their sloping branches, helps them to shed snow before it can break them.
Mina sees a tree that is bare, though it has needles in summer and cones like a pine. Tomas says that it is a larch, one of the few cone-bearing trees that drop all of their needles in winter.

Mina asks which way of getting through winter is better, and Tomas says that neither is. An evergreen can use mild days but needs tough needles, while a bare tree escapes the cold but must grow all its leaves again.
Tomas bends a snowy twig down so that Mina can see the tight brown buds along it. Inside each bud, wrapped in tough scales, are the folded leaves of next spring, which the tree prepared long ago.

On very cold nights, the water in a tree could freeze and tear its cells apart. Tomas says that before winter the tree changes the liquid in its cells, rather like antifreeze in a car, so the cold does little harm.
A squirrel is digging in the deep snow, and it finds a nut that it buried in autumn. Nearby a deer nibbles the end of a twig, and Tomas says that every nut the squirrel forgets might become a tree.

Mina brushes the snow carefully from her marker stick and thinks about the acorn that lies beneath it. Tomas says that many tree seeds need a spell of cold before they will sprout, so the winter is part of the plan.

A woodpecker is clinging to a tall grey trunk and hammering with its beak, and the sound echoes through the winter wood. The tree is dead, but it is covered with holes, and Tomas says that it is one of the busiest places in the forest.

Woodpeckers dig new holes each spring, and the old ones do not stay empty for long. Owls, bats, bees and small birds all move into them, because a hole in a dead tree is warm, dry and safe from most enemies.

Mina peels away a strip of loose bark and finds fine tunnels cut into the wood beneath it. Beetle larvae made them while they were feeding, and the woodpecker, which has a long tongue and sharp ears, knows exactly where to find them.
A pale, hard shelf is sticking out of the side of the trunk, and Mina taps it with her knuckle. Tomas says that it is the fruit of a fungus whose threads are slowly rotting the wood for many years.

Tomas tells her that scientists have counted the creatures that depend on dead wood in forests. In many woods it is about a fifth of all species, including beetles, fungi, birds and bats, so a dead tree is not wasted.
When Tomas was young, foresters cleared dead trees away to keep the wood neat. They found that this took away too many homes, so now many foresters leave some dead trees standing where it is safe.

Under a patch of moss, Mina finds a sleepy bumblebee queen, and nearby a ladybird is pressed into a crack in the bark. Many insects spend the cold months in a deep sleep, and the queen will start a new nest in spring.

A hazel dormouse is curled in a nest of leaves and grass, and Mina can just see its small, round shape. Tomas whispers that it lives on stored fat, and that waking it would waste energy it cannot spare, so they leave it alone.

A flock of blue tits is searching a bare hazel for tiny insects, and a robin hops along beside them. Small birds find food more easily in a group, because many eyes see more than two, and the robin sings even in the snow.

Back at the cottage, Mina warms her hands on a bowl of soup and opens her notebook. On a clean page she writes a heading, Things that look dead in winter, and fills half of it before her grandfather finishes eating.
Tomas kneels in the snow, scrapes away some soft earth and holds up a fine root for Mina to see. The root is wrapped in pale threads, and he tells her that they belong to a fungus.

Most of a fungus is not a mushroom but a web of threads so thin that you can hardly see them. Tomas says that a single pinch of forest soil may hold many metres of these threads, spreading through the dark in every direction.
The partnership between a fungus and a tree root has a long name, mycorrhiza. Tomas writes it in the snow and explains that it comes from two Greek words, meaning fungus and root.

The tree and the fungus do each other a favour, in what scientists call a trade. The tree sends sugar from its leaves down to the fungus, and the fungus sends water and minerals, such as phosphorus, back to the tree.

Mina draws a root hair and a fungal thread side by side in her notebook, and the thread is much the thinner of the two. The fine threads reach tiny gaps and water that roots cannot, so the tree can feed from far more soil.

Tomas says that most land plants have fungal partners of this kind, from tall trees to small ferns and flowers. The partnership is very old, and scientists have found traces of it in fossils more than four hundred million years old.

A single fungus does not usually stay with one tree, because its threads may touch the roots of several. Scientists have found that substances can pass along the threads from tree to tree, and in 1997 Suzanne Simard's team reported one such study.

Reporters have called the web of fungal threads the wood wide web, because it reminds them of the internet. Tomas says that the name is only a comparison, and a very useful one, but the forest is not a computer.
Mina closes her notebook and asks whether it means that the trees talk to each other. Tomas raises one finger and says that it is a lovely word, but talk may promise more than scientists know.

Under the great oak, small seedlings stand in its shade, and Tomas tells Mina about hub trees. Suzanne Simard, a forest scientist in Canada, noticed that some of the biggest and oldest trees were connected to many of their neighbours.
