One study hinted that a Douglas fir may treat its own seedlings a little differently from those of strangers. Tomas says that it is an exciting idea, and that it needs more careful work before anyone should be sure.

In 2023, a group of scientists looked at all of the research and said that some popular claims about forest networks went further than the evidence. Mina is surprised, but Tomas says that this is how science becomes more honest.
Mina asks who really benefits from the trade between the tree and the fungus. Tomas says that the fungus might keep a good share of the sugar, and a trade between partners is not always kind.

Many experiments are done with small plants in pots, which are very different from a real, wild forest. It is also hard to dig up threads without breaking them, so the results are difficult to carry over to the woods.
Tomas says that several things are agreed by almost everyone. Mycorrhizal fungi are real and trees depend on them, but how much passes along the threads, and whether it matters, is still debated.

Sitting on a snowy log, Mina draws three columns in her notebook and labels them known, probable and still unknown. She lists the fungal trade under known and the help for seedlings under probable, and she finds that the unknown column is the longest.

Tomas smiles when he sees her columns, and says that a good scientist is glad to write the words we do not know yet. Mina looks at the snow over her acorn and wonders whether threads are already reaching toward it.
The snow melts and drips from the branches, and a soft rain begins to fall on the buds. Mina hears a blackbird singing for the first time in months, and Tomas says that the forest is waking up.

Tomas shows her a birch tree with a small cut in its bark, where a drop of clear sap is slowly forming. In spring the sap rises through the tree, and in some countries people boil birch and maple sap to make sweet syrup.

Day by day, the buds on the oak swell, until the scales split and a tiny folded leaf appears. Mina watches the green spread through the wood like a slow wave, starting with the hawthorn and ending with the great beeches.
The days are longer and warmer now, and the forest floor is crowded with new life. A pale yellow butterfly rests on a primrose, and Tomas says that it spent the whole winter asleep as an adult.
Mina goes straight to her marker stick and kneels beside the acorn. The shell has split, and a pale, thick root has pushed out and turned downward into the soil.

Tomas explains that the root always comes out first, because the young plant needs to anchor itself and find water. The two halves of the acorn stay in the soil, and they feed the seedling until it has leaves of its own.

Tomas tells her that a root tip can sense which way is down, and that it bends to follow gravity. He suggests that Mina grows a bean in a glass jar at home, and turns the jar on its side to watch the root bend.

Mina uses her magnifying glass to look at the tip of a root that has come up with a weed. It is covered with fine white hairs, and Tomas says that these root hairs do most of the work of taking in water and minerals.

In the soil, a pale thread of fungus has found the tip of the young root. Tomas says that oak seedlings usually form partnerships with fungi already in the ground, so Mina's acorn may soon have its first partner.

Mina lays a small ruler beside the acorn and measures the new root, which is about two centimetres long. She draws it carefully in her notebook and writes the date beside it, and her grandfather says that she has become a real scientist.
Tomas takes a stick and draws the roots of the oak in the dust. They are not plunging straight down like a carrot, as Mina expected, but spreading wide and shallow beneath the surface.
Roots can sense where the soil is wetter, and they tend to grow in that direction. When they meet a stone, they simply grow around it and carry on, like a river that finds its way past a rock.
Tomas says that a tree's roots often spread out wider than its branches. Most of them lie in the top layer of soil, where the water, the air and the fungi are, and not far underground.
Mina's seedling begins with one long root that goes straight down, but the old oak looks different. As an oak grows older, it spreads wide with a mat of roots, and only a few thick roots go deep.
Roots do two jobs at once, and both are important for the tree. They hold it upright against the wind, and they hold the soil in place on hillsides, so that rain cannot wash it away.
Mina stamps on the path, and Tomas asks her to step more softly. Roots need air as well as water, and soil that is pressed hard by many boots has less room for either.
One morning Mina finds a small green shoot rising out of the soil beside her faded stick. It is bent like a hook at first, and then it straightens and opens its first small leaves.
The seedling stands at the edge of the old oak's shade, where the light is weak. Tomas says that oaks need plenty of light, so a seedling under a parent tree must be lucky to survive.

A deer has been browsing the young plants nearby and nibbled several of them to the ground. Mina's seedling is untouched, and Tomas says that an oak needs only one acorn out of its thousands to succeed in its lifetime.

Mina holds a small ruler beside the seedling, which is about five centimetres tall, and counts its leaves. Tomas says that a seedling in the shade may wait for years for more light, growing very slowly, so she should be patient.

The great oak has opened its new leaves, and the whole tree is now a cloud of fresh, bright green. Each leaf is soft and light at first, and hundreds of thousands of them will hang on a tree this size.

Mina stands under the oak and looks up, and sunlight shines through the leaves onto her face. Tomas says that every leaf is a tiny solar panel, because the chlorophyll inside it catches the light and puts it to work.

Tomas draws arrows on a page in her notebook: light, water and a gas called carbon dioxide go into the leaf. Sugar is made inside, and oxygen is given out, and the whole process is called photosynthesis.
Tomas tells her about van Helmont, who lived about four hundred years ago. He planted a small willow in a pot of weighed soil and watered it for five years, and then he weighed everything again.

The willow had gained more than seventy kilograms, but the soil had lost less than sixty grams. Van Helmont thought the tree was made from water, and he was partly right, but most of the new wood came from the air.
A tree is built mostly from carbon, and the carbon comes from carbon dioxide in the air. About half of dry wood is carbon, so Mina is surprised to learn that a trunk is largely made of air.
Trees give out oxygen as they make sugar, but Tomas says that they are not the only source. Ocean algae make a large share of the oxygen in the air, so the forest is not the lungs of the world.
The tree does not use all of its sugar for growth. It burns some of it to get energy, as an animal does, and it stores some as starch in its roots to use in winter.
Mina examines the underside of a leaf with her magnifying glass and sees the fine veins. Tomas says that tiny pores called stomata, far too small to see, are opened and closed by guard cells.
On a hot, dry afternoon, Mina's oak leaves look a little droopy, and she feels tired too. Tomas says that on days like this a tree closes its stomata to save water, and then it makes much less sugar.
Tomas points up the tall trunk and asks Mina how the water gets from the roots to the highest leaves. She cannot guess, because a tree has no heart to pump it, and Tomas smiles at her puzzled face.
The water travels through narrow tubes in the wood called xylem. When Tomas shows her a cut branch, she sees a bundle of fine, hollow tubes, like drinking straws packed side by side.

Water evaporates from the leaves into the air, and this pulls more water up behind it. Because water molecules cling to one another, the water forms an unbroken chain from the root to the leaf, and the whole column rises.

The tallest trees in the world are more than a hundred metres high. Scientists calculate that trees may not grow beyond about a hundred and twenty metres, because a longer column of water would break.

Mina asks how much water a tree really uses, and Tomas says that a large tree can lift hundreds of litres on a hot day. She imagines a row of full buckets beside the oak, and she realises that the tree is working all day.
Under the bark there is a second set of tubes, called phloem. They carry sugar from the leaves down to the roots, and also to the buds and growing tips, wherever the tree needs energy.

Tomas shows her a young tree with a ring of bark gnawed away around its trunk by hungry animals. Without its phloem, sugar cannot travel to the roots, so a tree that is stripped all the way around will often die.
Mina notices tiny green aphids on the underside of a leaf, drinking the sugary sap. They cannot use all of it, and they let drops of sweet liquid fall, which ants and bees collect.

Mina presses her ear against the oak and listens carefully, but she hears nothing. Scientists have recorded tiny clicks from trees in a drought, when the water columns break, but people cannot hear them without special instruments.

Tomas draws a loop in her notebook, with an arrow going up through the wood and another coming down through the bark. Mina adds the leaves at the top and the roots at the bottom, and she writes that the tree is a machine with no engine.
Mina wakes before dawn to the loudest birdsong of the year. At the edge of the clearing, a blue tit flies to a hole in the trunk with a beakful of moss for its nest.

A few weeks later, the same pair of blue tits is feeding a hole full of chicks. Tomas says that the chicks need thousands of caterpillars, so the parents time their nesting for when the caterpillars are most plentiful.

Tomas shows Mina a page of his old notebooks with two arrows on it, one for the oak leaves and one for the caterpillars. In very warm springs, the leaves and caterpillars can come earlier than the birds expect, so scientists watch the timing closely.
The oak has flowers, although Mina had never noticed them. Long yellow catkins hang from the twigs, and tiny female flowers sit beside them, so that one tree carries both kinds.
Tomas taps a branch, and a cloud of yellow dust rises into the sunshine. A tree that uses the wind has to make millions of grains, because most of them will never land on a flower.

On the willow catkins and the wild cherry blossom, the bees are working busily. Trees that depend on insects offer sweet nectar and bright flowers, so the bees visit them and carry pollen from one tree to the next.

Tomas tells Mina that some years the oak makes a huge crop of acorns and other years almost none. Scientists are still debating exactly how oaks decide, but a big crop means that animals cannot eat all of the acorns.

On the forest floor, bluebells and white wood anemones are in full bloom under the bare branches. They hurry to flower before the leaves above them open and close out the light, and then they will rest until next year.
A fluffy tawny owl chick sits on a low branch and gives a thin, squeaky call. Tomas says that the chick has left its nest hole early, and that its parents will keep feeding it in the dark.
One golden evening, Mina measures her seedling and finds that it is about ten centimetres tall, with six leaves. The days are long now, and she stays out until the light turns pink in the treetops.
A green caterpillar is chewing a lacy hole in a young oak leaf, and Mina watches it eat. Tomas says that the tree is not helpless, because oaks have several ways of defending themselves.

Mina feels something tickle her neck and finds a tiny caterpillar hanging by a silk thread. Winter moth caterpillars lower themselves from the branches on threads, and Tomas says that the wind carries them to new leaves.

The oak leaves are soft and tender in spring, and the caterpillars love them. As summer comes on, the leaves become tough, and they fill with bitter chemicals called tannins, which make them much harder to eat.

When a caterpillar bites a leaf, the damage sets off an alarm inside the tree. The alarm travels to other leaves, and some of them begin to make more bitter chemicals before the caterpillars reach them.
Mina tears a leaf in half and sniffs it, and she smells freshly cut grass. Tomas says that this smell is a mixture of chemicals that a damaged leaf gives off into the air.

In the 1980s, some scientists reported that trees near a damaged tree began to make more defences. Other scientists found it hard to repeat the results, and so people still debate how much it matters in a real forest.

A tiny wasp lands on a chewed leaf and begins to search for the caterpillar. Some wasps lay their eggs in caterpillars, and studies suggest that insect-eating birds are also drawn to trees that have been damaged.

Mina wonders if the forest is like a village where the trees warn each other. Tomas says that it is a lovely picture, but trees do not make plans, because evolution shaped these responses over a very long time.
On a twig, Mina finds a round brown ball, about the size of a marble, and Tomas calls it an oak apple. A tiny gall wasp laid an egg in a bud, and the tree grew a ball of tissue around the egg.
Tomas says that people have used oak galls to make ink for many centuries. He crushes one, mixes it with a little iron and water, and Mina writes her name in dark brown ink on a scrap of paper.
It is midsummer, and the fields beyond the trees are baking in the sun. Under the oak, beside the Stream, Mina and Tomas rest in a cool green room where the air feels soft and the light is dim.

Tomas has brought a small thermometer, and in the shade it reads several degrees lower than it did in the open field. Trees cool the air by blocking the sun and by releasing water vapour, which takes heat with it as it evaporates.

All the water that leaves the trees ends up in the air, and the forest feels damp and fresh. Some scientists think that big forests help to bring rain, because the water vapour they release can form clouds, though this is still being studied.

A sudden shower begins, and Mina and Tomas stand under the thick canopy, hardly getting wet. The leaves catch the first drops, and the rest trickles down the branches and the trunks, so the soil receives the water slowly.

Mina lifts a flat stone from the Stream, and a few tiny creatures hurry away from the sudden light. Tomas says that they are young mayflies and caddisflies, and that they can live only where the water is clean and cool.

Brown leaves from last autumn lie in the Stream, and a small grub is chewing at the edge of one. Many of the creatures in a stream depend on leaves from the forest, and so the food chain of the water begins with the trees.

A small brown bird called a dipper bobs on a wet stone and then walks right into the water. The shade of the trees keeps the Stream cool, and cool water holds more oxygen, which trout and many other animals need.
As the sky turns pink, small shapes begin to flicker over the clearing. They are bats, which sleep by day in tree holes, and a single bat can eat hundreds or even thousands of insects in a night.
At the edge of the forest, Mina sees tiny green lights glowing in the long grass. They are glow-worms, which are actually beetles, and the females glow so that the males can find them.

Mina and Tomas lie on a blanket and look up at the stars between the dark treetops. At night the oak stops making sugar, and scientists with lasers have measured some tree branches drooping a little in the dark.
A summer storm comes suddenly, and black clouds roll over the treetops. Mina and Tomas run to a rocky overhang and watch the wind bend the crowns of the trees.

Tomas says that wind is good for trees, because swaying makes a trunk grow thicker and stronger. Young trees held by stakes in a nursery often grow thin, and they fall over easily when the stakes are taken away.
Mina notices how different the trees look in the field beside the wood. A lone oak spreads wide in the open, but trees in a crowded forest grow tall and thin as they compete for light.

A flash of lightning lights up the forest, and Mina covers her ears before the thunder comes. Tomas says that tall trees are often struck, and that some of them survive with a long scar down the trunk.

After the storm, the forest drips and steams, and Mina and Tomas walk through the wet leaves. They find a giant beech lying on its side, with a great wall of roots and earth standing up where the tree once stood.
Mina touches the wall of roots and sees how shallow they are. Tomas says that a beech spreads its roots near the surface, and that on wet soil, a storm can topple even a very old tree.

A beam of sunlight falls through the hole in the canopy, and it lands exactly beside Mina's marker stick. Her seedling is standing in light for the first time, and she stares at it with her hand over her mouth.

New seedlings rush into the sunny gap, such as birch, rowan and bramble, which grow very fast. Tomas says that this is how a forest renews itself, and that it is a patchwork of places at different ages.
Near the Stream, Tomas touches a pine with a blackened scar running up its trunk. A fire went through here long ago, he says, but the tree survived, and green shoots are growing at its base.

Tomas tells Mina that in some pine forests, cones stay sealed with resin and open only in the heat of a fire. He adds that fire is natural in some places, but today many fires are too hot and too frequent for the trees to recover.
Months later, the great beech is still lying where it fell, but it hardly looks like a tree any more. It is covered in moss and ferns, and mushrooms push out of its bark in rows.
Mina finds a fat white grub inside the soft, rotten wood. Tomas says that it will become a stag beetle, and that some beetle larvae spend years inside a log before they come out.

Tomas explains that wood is very hard to digest, because it contains a tough substance called lignin. Only a few living things can break it down, and the fungi that rot wood are among the most important of them.

All along the back of the log, tiny trees are growing in a neat line, and Mina bends down to count them. Tomas says that a rotting log is called a nurse log, because it holds water, and raised seedlings may find more light there.

As the log rots, the carbon stored in its wood returns slowly to the air as carbon dioxide. Some of it also sinks into the soil, and so a fallen tree keeps its carbon for decades before it is released.
Mina reaches out to touch a pale mushroom, and Tomas gently stops her hand. He says that some wild mushrooms are deadly poisonous, and that nobody should eat one unless an expert has named it.

Tomas tells Mina that one honey fungus in the state of Oregon covers about nine square kilometres. Scientists think it may be thousands of years old, which would make it one of the largest living things on Earth.

Mina notices that honey-coloured mushrooms are growing around the base of a young tree that is dying. Tomas says that not all fungi are friends, and that honey fungus can attack living trees as well as dead ones.

Tomas tells her about Dutch elm disease, which is caused by a fungus carried by bark beetles. In the last century it killed many millions of elm trees across Europe and North America, and the great elms of many towns disappeared.

Beside a bare ash tree, Mina writes in her notebook while a thin fog drifts through the wood. Tomas says that disease can now travel the world with trade, and that scientists are searching for trees that resist it.

On a rainy evening, Tomas takes down a heavy book from the shelf and opens it on the kitchen table. It shows a twisted old pine on a dry mountain, and he says that it is one of the oldest living things on Earth.

The tree is a bristlecone pine, and these trees grow high in the dry mountains of the western United States. Some of them are almost five thousand years old, which means that they were already growing when the pyramids of Egypt were being built.

Bristlecone pines live so long because they grow very slowly in cold, dry places where few things can harm them. Their wood is full of resin, which resists rot and insects, and an old tree may keep only a thin strip of living bark.

Scientists matched the rings of living bristlecones with the rings of old dead wood lying on the ground. This gave them a record of the weather and the years that goes back thousands of years, much further than any one tree could reach.

Tomas turns the page and shows Mina a picture of the coast redwoods, which grow along the foggy Pacific coast of California. They are the tallest trees in the world, and the tallest of them are over a hundred metres high.

Redwood roots are shallow but wide, and they join the roots of neighbouring trees so that the grove holds itself up. High in the crowns of the oldest redwoods, there are even patches of soil, and small animals live there all their lives.
Autumn has come around again, and the leaves of the oak are turning gold. Mina and Tomas walk through the falling leaves, and she realises that she has now seen every season of the forest.

Mina hurries to the place where the stick stands, now faded to grey, and she kneels and looks into the grass. There, beside it, is her seedling, a year older and still alive, with a small bud already formed for the spring.

The little oak is still very small, but the gap left by the fallen beech has given it more light than most seedlings ever get. Tomas says that it may take many years to reach the canopy, and that it must be patient.

Tomas puts three seeds on Mina's palm: a tiny redwood seed, a bristlecone seed and an acorn. The giants of the world all began like this, he says, and Mina's oak is just at the beginning of its own long story.

Mina presses both hands against a trunk and feels the sun warming the leaves above. Tomas says that as trees grow, they take carbon dioxide from the air and store its carbon in their wood, roots and soil.

When forests are burned or cleared, much of their stored carbon goes back into the air as the gas that is warming the planet. Tomas says that keeping old forests standing is among the most useful things people can do, although it cannot replace cutting pollution.
Mina sees a deer step out of the trees to drink at the clear Stream. She holds her breath, and Tomas says that forests also shelter animals, hold the soil and keep the water clean.

Tomas tells Mina that planting trees helps, especially the right kinds in the right places. Not every open place should become a wood, because some grasslands and bogs are precious habitats of their own.
Protecting old forests is just as important as planting new ones. Their soil, their fungi and their ancient trees cannot easily be replaced, because they took centuries to build.

On a bright day in the village, Mina and her neighbours plant a young tree in a sunny field. She digs the hole with Tomas and presses the soil down around the roots, and her hands are dirty and happy.
On their last walk, Tomas gives Mina two simple rules. Leave deadwood where it lies, because many creatures live in it, and walk lightly, because crushed soil is hard on roots.

That evening, Mina reads her whole notebook from the first page, and she smiles at the first line, one acorn. Her three columns have changed, because many things that were unknown a year ago are now known to her.

The next morning, Mina walks alone along the path where her year began, and the leaves rustle around her boots. Under the oak she finds a sound, heavy acorn with its cap still on, and she decides to plant it.
Mina plants the acorn in a sunny gap at the edge of the forest and pushes a new stick in beside it. She may never see it grow old, but Tomas says that a forest is made by people who plant for others.

Everything he was about to tell her, he said, had been found out by patient scientists with notebooks, and she was welcome to ask about any of it.

A shallow Stream crossed the path, and Tomas led her over it on flat stepping stones while the last of the mist drifted off the water like breath. An old forest has its own rules, he said, and the first of them is that nobody who is in a hurry ever sees anything. Mina, who had been about to run ahead, put her feet down more carefully and began to listen.

Beyond the water stood an oak so vast that Mina's outstretched arms covered barely a third of its trunk, and its lowest branches were thicker than most trees in a garden. Tomas guessed that it had stood there for more than two hundred years, judging by the old maps of the estate, although he admitted that nobody had written down the day it began. She tipped her head back to look for the top of the crown, but the branches closed overhead and hid it.

Every few moments an acorn dropped from the branches, struck the leaves below with a small, dry tap, and rolled away into the shadows like a runaway bead. Oaks, Tomas told her, do not give the same harvest every year, for in some seasons they let fall an astonishing number of acorns and in others almost none at all. Scientists still debate exactly what signals tell a whole wood when to do it together.

Tomas picked up a fresh acorn, slid his knife around it with great care, and held the two halves out on his open palm. Inside lay a minute, pale shape that was already the beginning of a tree, packed in beside the thick store of food that would feed it until its first leaves could catch the light. Mina bent so close that her breath fogged the tiny thing, and he told her that this was the whole secret of a seed.

A squirrel went whisking along a fallen branch, a deer lifted its head at the edge of the clearing, and somewhere in the leaves a field mouse was busily at work. Acorns are among the richest foods in an autumn wood, Tomas explained, and so pigeons, boar, mice and a dozen other creatures depend on them. It followed that the great majority of the acorns Mina could see would end their lives as someone's dinner rather than as oaks.

A jay dropped out of the branches with a harsh, rattling cry, snatched up an acorn and then another, and stored them in its throat until its neck swelled. Then it was off between the trunks, and Tomas said that a single jay may carry thousands of acorns in a season, often to places far beyond the shade of the parent tree. Mina watched the blue and white flash of its wing until the forest closed behind it.

The jay reappeared a little farther on and pushed an acorn deep into the soil with its beak, covering it with a leaf as neatly as a person tucking in a child. Birds like this recover most of what they hide, Tomas said, but never all of it, and the acorns they forget can sprout in places the oak could never have reached on its own. A forest, then, is planted partly by creatures that have simply lost track of their own pantries, and Mina decided that she approved.

Mina knelt by the trunk and found a single acorn already half sunk into the damp soil, its shell still shining as if it had been polished. She pushed a stick into the ground beside it, so that she could find it again, and made herself a quiet promise to visit it in every season of the year. It was a very small beginning, but she felt as though she were holding a very large secret.

That evening, in the kitchen of the cottage at the forest's edge, Mina opened a fresh notebook, wrote the date at the top of the page and added two words underneath: one acorn. Tomas looked over her shoulder and asked her, very seriously, what she thought it would be by the next autumn, and she chewed the end of her pencil for a long time. In the end she wrote a question mark, which, he told her, is the way every good scientist begins.

Mina held a single yellow leaf up against a hillside of crimson and orange, comparing it with the trees as though she were matching paint. She had always taken autumn colour for granted, but now she wanted to know what exactly was happening, and she put the question to her grandfather without hesitation. Tomas looked pleased, because it was the sort of question he had been hoping she would ask.

The green of a summer leaf comes from chlorophyll, Tomas explained, a pigment that absorbs red and blue light and reflects the green, and uses the light it captures to help make food for the tree. It works so busily in summer that its colour drowns out everything else in the leaf. Mina held the leaf up to the sun and tried to imagine the tiny green factory within it.

As the days shorten and the nights turn cool, the tree gradually stops making new chlorophyll, and the old supply breaks down faster than it can be replaced. The green therefore drains out of the leaf slowly, like colour from a fading photograph, and the tree makes this change in response to the length of the night rather than to any single cold morning. Mina thought it remarkable that a tree could keep such careful track of the calendar.

Beneath the green, Tomas said, the leaf has carried yellow and orange pigments for the whole of the summer, and they were only waiting to be uncovered. Mina picked up one pale leaf and one golden one and laid them side by side on her palm, amazed that colours which seemed so new had been hidden there all along. It is a little like discovering that a plain wall has had a painting under it for months.

Red, on the other hand, is a latecomer, because many trees manufacture a fresh red pigment in the leaf as autumn comes on. Scientists have offered several explanations, among them that it may act as a sunscreen for the leaf or help the tree to recover its nutrients, but the question remains open, and Tomas liked it all the better for that. Mina thought it was good to know that even something so beautiful could still be a puzzle.

Mina began sorting the fallen leaves into little heaps on the path, and soon she had worked out that each kind of tree keeps its own palette. Oak leaves turned mostly a dull russet brown, beech leaves glowed like new copper, and a few maples by the Stream had burned a fierce red. Tomas said that a good forester could name a wood from a distance in October simply by the pattern of its colours.

Tomas held up a leaf that was yellow on one half and still faintly green on the other, and told her that the tree was not simply throwing its leaves away. Before it lets go, the tree draws back much of the valuable material that the leaf contains, including nutrients that were hard to find in the soil, and stores them in its branches and roots until spring. Nothing in a forest, Mina was beginning to see, is wasted if it can possibly be saved.

At the base of every leaf stalk the tree builds a thin layer of cells, which weakens the join and at the same time seals the twig like a plug. When the work is complete, the leaf hangs by hardly anything at all, and the slightest breath of wind can send it spinning to the ground. Mina examined a bare twig and found a row of neat, tiny scars where the leaves had been, each one closed as if by a careful hand.

A broad, thin leaf gives away water continually, Tomas said, and in winter, with the ground frozen, the roots cannot drink fast enough to replace it. Heavy snow would also settle on a full crown of leaves and tear the branches from the tree, so by letting its leaves drop, the oak protects itself against drought and against weight at the same time. Mina looked at the bare, patient branches above her with new respect, as though they had suddenly become wise.

Soon the whole floor of the wood was a thick and rustling carpet, and Mina dragged her boots through it for the sheer pleasure of the noise. She pressed an oak leaf and a beech leaf between the pages of her notebook, labelled them carefully, and breathed in the smell of earth and damp that rose around her. Pine trees, Tomas said, with a mysterious smile, had quite a different way of getting through the winter, and she would see it before long.

Mina lifted a layer of sodden leaves with the tip of her stick and found an entire hidden city underneath. Worms, beetles and small pale creatures she could not name were crawling through the dark litter, going about their business as though she did not exist. Tomas crouched beside her and said that the forest floor, in autumn, is among the busiest places in the world.

An earthworm was hauling a leaf down into a narrow burrow, tugging it by the tip until it vanished into the soil like a flag lowered at sunset. Tomas told her that Charles Darwin had spent years watching earthworms and had written a whole book on the subject, in which he showed how much soil they move and mix over the course of a lifetime. Mina found it comforting that one of the most famous scientists in history had once knelt exactly where she was kneeling.

Springtails, mites and woodlice were chewing the fallen leaves into smaller and smaller fragments, and Mina could hardly believe how many of them there were in the space of a single handprint. A springtail is so small that she could only see it when it jumped, flicking itself into the air with a spring folded beneath its body. These tiny creatures, Tomas said, do the first rough work of breaking a leaf down, and they do it without anyone ever thanking them.

Across a half-rotten leaf spread a fine white web of threads, so delicate that Mina's breath seemed to disturb it. This was fungus, Tomas said, and it feeds by releasing chemicals that dissolve the leaf from the outside and then soaking up the nourishment that is set free. Where the threads had passed, the leaf was soft and brown and ready to fall to pieces at a touch.

Tomas scooped up a handful of dark soil and held it out for her to see, telling her that it was thick with living things too small to be seen by the naked eye. Bacteria carry out a huge share of the work of decay, he said, and a single spoonful of healthy forest soil may contain billions of them. Mina stared at the crumbs in her hand, and for the first time in her life soil did not look like plain dirt.

Mina compared three leaves from three places along the path: one almost whole, one riddled with holes, and one that was no more than a skeleton of brown lace. A leaf may need a year or more to be turned into soil, Tomas said, and the speed depends on the kind of leaf and on how warm and damp the ground happens to be. She laid them in a row on a log, like a small museum of slow disappearance.

The nutrients locked inside last year's leaves were slowly being released, and the soil was taking them back, ready to be used again. Tomas pointed up at the oak and said that its roots would draw some of that wealth in once more, so that the tree was partly fed by the remains of its own old leaves. A forest, Mina realised, is a place that has been recycling for far longer than any person has.

Mina knelt on the path and breathed in the smell of the damp earth, a rich, dark scent that reminded her of rain falling on a dusty road. Part of that smell, Tomas told her, comes from a chemical made by certain soil bacteria, and people are so good at noticing it that they can detect it in very tiny amounts. She wondered what use such a talent could ever have been, and he said that perhaps it was simply a pleasure.

Between two roots a small brown mushroom had pushed up through the wet leaves, its cap still wearing a few crumbs of soil like a hat. Tomas explained that a mushroom is only the fruit of a fungus, in the way an apple is only the fruit of an apple tree, and that the real body of the fungus lies out of sight in the ground. Mina was careful not to touch it, and Tomas said that was exactly right.

Mina went back to her marker stick and found that the wind had blown a few of the leaves off the acorn. She tucked them back with great care, and Tomas, watching, told her that a blanket of leaves keeps the frost out of the soil and helps to hold the moisture in. It struck her that she was doing, in a small way, what the forest did on its own all the time.

Tomas tilted his head back and pointed up through the treetops, showing Mina that a forest is built in layers like a tall house with rooms at every height. Right at the top lies the canopy, below it the understorey, and at the bottom the forest floor, and each of them has its own light, its own air and its own residents. She followed his finger from the crowns to the ferns, and for the first time the forest seemed to have an architecture.

The canopy, Tomas said, is the roof of the forest, a layer of leaves spread out by the crowns of the tallest trees to catch the sunlight before anything else can. The trees up there live in brilliant light and are lashed by wind and rain, while everything below must make do with whatever light slips through the gaps. Mina squinted into the glare and thought that it must be the best room in the building and also the loneliest.

Beneath the canopy grows a second layer of smaller trees and shrubs such as hazel, holly and hawthorn, which scientists call the understorey. Some of these plants will never grow any larger, but others are the young of the great trees, waiting in the shade for the day when an old giant falls and opens a space above them. Mina realised that the understorey was partly a waiting room, and she wondered how long some of them had been sitting there.

On the forest floor it was dim and cool, and the air smelled of moss and wet stone, for only a small fraction of the sunlight that strikes the canopy ever reaches the ground. A few ferns, some patches of moss and a handful of flowers have learned to live on that meagre ration, and Tomas said that many of them hurry through their lives in spring, before the leaves above have fully opened. A single bar of light fell across Mina's boots, and she stepped out of it, feeling that she had taken someone else's seat.

High in the trunk of the oak, Mina noticed a round, dark hole where a branch had broken off many years ago and the wood had rotted inside. A tawny owl might sleep there by day, Tomas said, while beetles and worms were working at the soil far below, so that nearly every height in the wood had its own tenants. She searched the edges of the hole for feathers, but the owl, if it was home, kept perfectly hidden.

Several beech trunks leaned slightly in the same direction, as though they were listening to something beyond the edge of the wood, towards a gap in the leafy roof where the sunlight poured through. Trees growing close together are in a constant race for light, Tomas said, and so they put all of their effort into height and keep nearly all of their leaves right at the top. Mina saw that the straight, bare trunks were less like pillars and more like the long legs of runners.

Mina laid her palm on a beech and felt smooth, cool grey bark, and then crossed to the oak and felt the thick ridges that seemed to be carved from stone. Bark works like skin, Tomas told her, protecting the living wood beneath from frost, from hungry insects, from rot and sometimes even from fire, and the different kinds of tree have invented different kinds of armour. A good forester, he added, can name a tree in the dark simply by touching its bark.

Tomas picked up a loose strip of bark from the ground and showed her the damp, pale surface on its inner side, which was streaked with fine channels. Just beneath the bark lies a thin layer where the tree truly grows, he said, adding a little new wood to the inside and a little new bark to the outside every single year. She turned the strip over in her fingers and was amazed that the whole bulk of the tree was made by something thinner than a sheet of paper.

Patches of green moss and pale grey lichen were scattered over the bark, softening the shape of the trunk as though someone had begun to knit it a coat. A lichen is not a single organism, Tomas explained, but a partnership between a fungus and an alga, and moss will grow wherever it is damp, which is why the old tale about moss pointing north cannot be trusted. Mina decided that the best compasses were still the ones with needles, and tucked the thought away for later.

Mina leaned her cheek against the cold bark of the oak and looked up along the trunk, which seemed to go on and on until it was lost among the branches. Most of what she was looking at was old, dead wood that served only to hold the tree up, Tomas said, for only a thin outer skin is alive and growing at any moment. It was an odd thought that a tree could be so large and so old and still be mostly a monument built by a thin layer of living cells.

Beside the path lay a freshly cut stump, still pale and smelling faintly of resin, and Mina bent over it and began to count the circles with her fingertip. Tomas explained that the tree had been leaning dangerously over the path and had to be taken down for safety, and that it was a pity but not a tragedy. She counted slowly, losing her place twice and starting again, until she reached sixty-one.

On closer inspection, every ring turned out to be made of two parts: a broad pale band that the tree grew quickly in spring, and a thinner, darker band that it added more slowly in summer. The two together make one year of growth, Tomas said, and in the cold months the tree adds nothing at all, which is why the bands are separated so clearly. Mina ran her nail along the boundary between one year and the next and felt the faintest ridge.

Mina rested her finger on the very centre of the stump, where the first tiny ring was no bigger than a coin, and Tomas said that it had been laid down when he was a schoolboy. He was quiet for a while, and she guessed that he was thinking of everything that had happened to him in the sixty years since. The tree had been there through all of it, adding its patient circles, without ever having been asked to keep a record.

Some of the rings were wide and pale and others were narrow and tight, and Tomas said that they were a diary the tree had written without meaning to. A wide ring usually means a good year of water and warmth, a thin one a hard year, and a trunk is therefore a record of weather that nobody was measuring at the time. Mina touched the narrowest ring with one finger and wondered what that long-ago year had been like for the tree.

Tomas told her that scientists compare the patterns of wide and narrow rings from many trees, rather as a detective compares fingerprints, and so can trace the sequence back through centuries of old timber. By this method they can work out the year in which a beam in an ancient church roof was cut from the forest, which is sometimes a great help to historians. Mina thought it extraordinary that a piece of wood could carry a date inside it.

Mina marked one particularly narrow ring with her pencil and asked what had happened that year, and Tomas replied that it might have been a drought, or even a cold summer after a great volcanic eruption far away. Researchers have found such patterns in the rings of many trees, he said, and they use them with care, because a single narrow ring can have more than one cause. She felt that she was being let in on a very old and very patient kind of detective work.

Farther along the path a beech trunk had grown right over a rusty nail, so that only a faint ridge of bark showed where the metal had been driven in. A tree cannot heal a wound as skin does, Tomas explained, for it never repairs the damaged wood but seals it in and grows new layers over the top, and so every injury stays in the trunk for ever. Mina found it strangely moving that a tree should keep its scars so honestly.

Tomas split a short log with a wedge to show her the heart of a trunk, where the wood was a darker colour and as hard as a stone. This heartwood no longer carries water, he said, but its dense, dead cells hold the tree upright, while the pale outer ring called sapwood does the work of lifting water to the leaves. That, he added, is why an old tree can be hollow and still live for a century, since the living part lies near the outside.

On a smooth grey beech, Mina found a letter T cut deep into the bark, its edges stretched and softened by many seasons of growth. Tomas confessed that he had carved it as a boy, and she was astonished to see that it was no higher than the top of her head, when she had expected it to have risen with the tree. A tree grows taller only at the tips of its shoots, he told her, so a mark made on the trunk stays at exactly the height where it was cut.

One morning the grass crunched under their boots and the last of the leaves on the ground were stiff with the first white frost of the year. Mina wrote the date in her notebook and drew a small snowflake beside it, and Tomas, watching the breath rise from her mouth, said that the forest was about to go very quiet. She did not yet understand how much would be going on beneath the stillness.

Snow began to fall in slow, heavy flakes that settled on the shoulders of Mina's coat, and she and Tomas pulled their wool hats down over their ears and set out between the bare trunks. The wood had gone white and astonishingly silent, as though someone had turned the sound down, and the only noise was the creak of their boots and the occasional soft slump of snow from a branch. Mina felt that she was walking through a very large and very careful room.

To Mina the bare trees looked dead, but Tomas showed her a simple test, and she scratched a twig with her thumbnail until a thin line of moist green appeared beneath the bark. The tree was not dead at all, he said, only resting, and the living layer under the skin was waiting patiently for the days to lengthen. She covered the scratch with her glove, as if she had wounded a sleeping animal and wished to say sorry.

Pine trees, Tomas said, handle the winter differently from oaks, for they keep their needles all year round and are therefore called evergreens. Each needle is narrow and wrapped in a waxy coat that holds in water, so the tree loses very little to the cold, dry air, even while the ground around its roots is frozen. Mina touched one and found that it felt smooth and slightly sticky, like a small candle.

A heavy cushion of snow lay along a pine branch until the branch bent under the weight and tipped it off in a soft white cloud that settled on Mina's hat. The sloping shape of many evergreens, with their flexible, drooping boughs, is a clever way of shedding snow before it can do any damage, Tomas said, and spruces in the far north are often shaped like narrow church spires. Mina brushed the powder from her face and laughed, delighted that the forest had thrown the first snowball.

Among the dark pines Mina spotted a tree that had lost every needle, and which stood bare and golden-brown against the snow like a wire sculpture of itself. This was a larch, Tomas said, one of the very few cone-bearing trees that drop their needles in autumn and grow fresh ones in spring, and he added that nature rarely follows a rule without making at least one exception. She was glad of the exception, because it meant that nobody could ever claim to have worked out the forest.

Mina asked which of the two ways of getting through winter was the better, and Tomas answered that neither is, since each costs the tree something. An evergreen can make food on any mild day but must build needles that last for years, whereas a tree that drops its leaves escapes the cold but must grow a whole new crop each spring. Mina thought it was an excellent reminder that in nature the question is rarely which is best, but which is best here.

Tomas bent a snowy twig down so that Mina could see the small, tight buds along its length, each sealed in overlapping scales against the frost. Inside every bud, he told her, the tree had folded the leaves of next spring months earlier, so that nothing would be left to chance when the warm weather returned. She held the twig very gently, feeling that she was holding a promise that the whole forest had made to itself.

Frost sparkled on every branch, and Mina's breath went up in a white cloud, and she asked how a tree could stand being frozen for a whole winter without being torn to pieces. Tomas explained that in the autumn the tree alters the liquid inside its cells, so that ice forms where it can do no harm, in much the way that a driver puts antifreeze in a car. Mina felt colder just thinking about it, but she was filled with admiration for the stubborn, clever trees.

A squirrel was digging furiously in the deep snow, and with a flick of its tail it turned up a nut that it had buried in the autumn. A deer stood a little way off, nibbling the end of a twig with great delicacy, while a trail of tiny prints crossed the clearing and vanished among the roots. Tomas whispered that every nut the squirrel failed to find was a possible tree, and Mina decided that forgetfulness may be one of the forest's most useful habits.

Mina brushed the snow carefully from her marker stick, and stood for a while thinking of the acorn lying hidden beneath her boots in the frozen ground. Tomas told her that many kinds of tree seed need a spell of cold before they will sprout, which keeps them from germinating during a warm spell in autumn and then being killed by the real winter. The cold, he said, is part of the plan, and she nodded as if the acorn could hear.

A woodpecker was clinging to a tall grey trunk and hammering at it with its beak, and the rattling sound carried a long way through the winter wood. The tree was quite dead, with no bark left on the upper branches and holes all over its sides, yet Tomas said that it was one of the busiest places in the forest. Mina looked closely and saw that he was right, for something was moving in or out of nearly every hole.

Woodpeckers chisel out new nest holes each spring, Tomas explained, and the old ones never stay vacant for long. Owls, bats, wild bees and many small birds all move in afterwards, because a hole in a dead trunk is warm, dry and safe from most predators, and the woodpecker, in effect, is the builder of half the neighbourhood. Mina counted six holes in one tree and wondered who lived behind every door.

Mina peeled a strip of loose, dry bark from the trunk and found a pattern of fine tunnels etched into the pale wood, radiating outward like the lines of a map. Beetle grubs had cut them while feeding beneath the bark, Tomas said, and the woodpecker, with its keen ears and long, barbed tongue, knows exactly where to look for such a meal. She put the bark down carefully, feeling that she had been reading somebody's private letter.

A pale, hard shelf stuck out from the side of the trunk, and Mina tapped it with her knuckle and found that it was as solid as a piece of wood. It was the fruit of a fungus, Tomas explained, whose hidden threads were rotting the dead wood from inside, a process that would take many years and was, as far as the forest was concerned, entirely beneficial. Some of the fungus's work would end up in the soil, and some of it would end up in the bodies of beetles.

Tomas told her that scientists have counted the creatures that rely on dead wood, and that in many European woods roughly a fifth of all species depend on it, among them beetles, fungi, birds and bats. A dead tree is therefore not a wasted tree but a block of flats, and Mina, who had always imagined a forest as a place of living things, saw that death was one of its most important residents. She wrote the figure down in her notebook, with the word roughly underlined twice, to be on the safe side.

When Tomas was a young man, he said, foresters used to clear dead trees out of the woods to keep them neat and to avoid disease, and he had done a great deal of that work himself. They have since learned that this took away the homes of too many creatures, and now many foresters leave some dead trees standing wherever it is safe, a change of mind that still embarrasses him a little. Mina told him that changing your mind when you find out more is exactly what scientists do, and he looked pleased.

Beneath a clump of moss, Mina found a sleepy bumblebee queen with her legs tucked in, and nearby a ladybird had wedged itself into a crack in the bark. A great many insects spend the winter in a deep sleep in such hiding places, Tomas said, and the bumblebee queen alone survives to start a new nest when the warm weather returns. Mina covered the moss gently, as a person might replace the lid of a box that holds something fragile.

In a nest of leaves and grass among the roots of a hazel lay a dormouse, curled into a tight, golden-brown ball, and Mina caught her breath at the sight of it. It was hibernating, Tomas whispered, living on fat stored in its body, and if she woke it, it would burn precious energy that it could not replace before spring. They backed away on tiptoe, and Mina found that she was holding her breath, as if even that might be too loud.

A flock of blue tits was searching the bare hazel branches for tiny insects and eggs, calling to each other in thin, bright voices, and a robin hopped along the fence beside them. Small birds find food more easily in a group, Tomas said, because many eyes see more than a single pair and one bird that finds a feast soon tells the others. The robin, which defends its own patch and does not join the flock, sang a few clear notes from a branch, quite unbothered by the snow.

Back at the cottage, Mina warmed her hands on a bowl of soup, and then opened her notebook and wrote a heading at the top of a clean page: Things that look dead in winter. By the time her grandfather had finished eating, she had filled half the page, with the twigs, the dormouse, the queen bumblebee and the acorn, and she could already see that the list would never end. He read it over her shoulder and told her that this was exactly how a naturalist's notebook begins.

Tomas knelt in the snow, scraped away a little of the soft earth beneath the leaf litter, and lifted out a fine root for Mina to see. Wrapped around its tip was a delicate sleeve of pale threads, like a glove made from cobwebs, and he told her that these were part of a fungus that was living in partnership with the tree. Mina bent so close that her breath made the threads tremble, and she held very still to see them settle.

The mushrooms Mina had seen in autumn were only the fruit of the fungus, Tomas said, and the greater part of the fungus is a web of threads so fine that they can scarcely be seen without a lens. A single pinch of forest soil may hold many metres of them, running in every direction through the dark, so that the ground beneath her boots was as much a fabric as a surface. She stood still, and for a moment felt a little bit afraid to step.

The partnership between a fungus and a tree root has a name that is a mouthful, mycorrhiza, which Tomas wrote in the snow with a stick as he said it. It comes from two Greek words, one meaning fungus and the other meaning root, and it describes a shared life so ancient and so ordinary that it exists almost everywhere there are trees. Mina repeated the word three times until she could say it without stumbling, and then a fourth time for luck.

The two partners, Tomas explained, are engaged in a kind of trade: the tree sends some of its sugar down to the fungus, and the fungus sends water and minerals, such as phosphorus, back up to the tree. Neither could easily manage so well alone, for the fungus cannot make sugar and the tree cannot reach everything it needs in the soil. Mina thought that it sounded like a very old and very successful business, with no complaints on either side.

In her notebook, Mina drew a root hair and a fungal thread side by side, and the thread was far thinner, so that it looked like a hair next to a rope. Because the threads are so fine, they can reach the tiniest cracks in the soil and tap pockets of water that a root could never enter, so a tree with fungal partners feeds from a far wider stretch of ground. She added an arrow to the page and wrote the word reach beside it, underlining it twice.

Most land plants have fungal partners of this kind, Tomas said, from the tallest trees to the smallest ferns and flowers, and the partnership is astonishingly old. Scientists have found traces of fungi inside the fossil roots of plants that lived more than four hundred million years ago, which suggests that the partnership may have helped plants to take to the land in the first place. Mina put her hand flat on the snow and felt, for the first time, that she was touching something very ancient.

One well-known kind of mycorrhizal fungus produces the truffle, which forms underground, close to the roots of oak and hazel trees, and which has such a powerful smell that people train dogs to find it. The part of the fungus that people eat is only its fruit, Tomas reminded her, and the real organism, like the others, is the web of threads in the soil. Mina laughed at the thought of a dog, nose to the ground, hunting for the fruit of a fungus under her own oak.

A single fungus is rarely loyal to one tree, Tomas said, for its threads can touch the roots of several trees at once and so join them in a shared network. Scientists have measured substances moving along the threads from one tree to another, and in 1997 Suzanne Simard and her colleagues reported one of the first studies showing that carbon appeared to pass between trees of different species. Mina wrote the year in her notebook with great care, as if the discovery had happened only yesterday.

Reporters have sometimes called this tangle of threads the wood wide web, because it makes them think of the internet, with trees as the computers and the fungus as the cable. Tomas said that the name is only a comparison, and a vivid one that has helped many people become curious, but that a forest is not a machine and that its connections are far less tidy than wires. Mina smiled, but she resolved not to say it in front of any scientist without a pinch of caution.

Mina closed her notebook and asked whether all this meant that the trees were talking to one another. Tomas raised one finger and told her that it was a lovely word, but one that might promise more than scientists really know, because a substance passing between two trees is not the same thing as a conversation. She asked him what word he would use instead, and he said that he was still looking for it.

Standing beneath the great oak, where a handful of small seedlings crowded in its shade, Tomas told Mina about hub trees and about the Canadian scientist Suzanne Simard. Simard and her colleagues had noticed that some of the biggest and oldest trees in a forest seemed to be linked to an unusually large number of their neighbours, and they called these giants hub trees and mother trees. Tomas said that the second name is poetic, and that scientists argue about whether it is the right one.

To find out which trees were joined to which, the researchers read the DNA of the fungi growing on the roots in a stand of Douglas fir trees, and from it they drew a kind of map of the connections. On the map, a few of the largest trees showed up as hubs with a great many threads, while the smaller trees seemed to hang on the edges of the network like villages along a railway. Mina studied the diagram that Tomas sketched in the snow and thought it looked like a plan of the underground itself.

Some experiments suggest that seedlings connected into the network of an older tree may grow better than those left alone, especially in shade, where light is scarce and a little help could matter a great deal. The idea is that sugar or nutrients might travel along the fungal threads to the young plants, though Tomas stressed that the amounts involved are small and that the results are not the same in every forest. He spoke the way people speak when they are trying very hard not to promise too much.

One study went further and hinted that a Douglas fir may treat its own seedlings a little differently from the seedlings of strangers, as though the tree could recognise its relatives. Tomas called it a fascinating idea, one that scientists found exciting, but he said it needed much more careful testing before anyone could say so with confidence. Mina wrote the word relatives in her notebook and added a question mark that was almost as large as the word itself.

In 2023, a group of scientists examined a large body of research on these networks and concluded that some of the most popular claims about them had gone beyond the evidence. They did not say that the networks do not exist, only that a few exciting results had been repeated so often in books and films that people had begun to treat them as settled facts. Mina was surprised, but Tomas said that this kind of honest checking is how science becomes more trustworthy, not less.

Mina asked who truly benefits from all this trading, and Tomas replied that this is another open question, because the fungus might keep a great deal of the sugar for itself and pass on only what it must. A trade between partners need not be an act of kindness, he said, any more than a shop is kind to its customers, and it would be a mistake to see the forest as one big loving family. Mina said that she would rather see it as a market, and he laughed and said that she might be nearer the truth.

Many of the experiments, Tomas continued, are carried out on small plants in pots, which are a long way from the tangle of a real forest with its thousands of competing roots and its changing weather. It is also very difficult to dig up the threads without breaking them, so scientists must work from small samples and clever tricks, and the results are hard to carry over to the woods. Mina understood that the difficulty was not carelessness but the sheer hidden size of the thing they were studying.

Tomas laid out what was agreed: mycorrhizal fungi are real and very important, trees depend on them, and the threads can physically join many trees. What is still debated is how much actually passes along the threads, whether it makes any difference to a tree in a wild forest, and whether the old trees really act as nurses to the young ones. He said that the debate was healthy, and that it was exactly where the most interesting science was happening.

Sitting on a snowy log, Mina drew three columns in her notebook and labelled them known, probable and still unknown, then began to sort everything she had learned that day. She put the fungal trade and the physical links under known, the help for seedlings under probable, and she noticed with a kind of delight that the third column was by far the longest. A list of questions, she thought, is a much more exciting thing to own than a list of answers.

Tomas smiled when he saw the columns, and said that a good scientist is happy to write the words we do not know yet and does not feel ashamed of them. Mina looked at the white ground where her acorn lay hidden and wondered whether some pale threads had already begun reaching out toward it in the dark. It was a question that nobody could answer from the surface, and she found that she did not mind at all.

The snow shrank back from the roots of the trees, the branches dripped with meltwater, and a soft rain began to fall on the swelling buds. Somewhere in the hazel a blackbird sang a few liquid notes, the first Mina had heard in months, and Tomas stopped on the path with his head tilted as if listening to an old friend. The forest was waking, he said, and it was a good idea to be there at the moment it happened.

Beside the path stood a birch with a neat little cut in its bark, and from the cut hung a single bright drop of clear sap. In spring, Tomas explained, the sap begins to rise through the tree again, and in colder countries people tap birch and maple trees and boil the sap down into syrup, using a great many litres for a single jar. Mina caught the drop on her fingertip and found that it tasted of almost nothing, only a faint, cool sweetness.

Day by day the buds on the oak swelled, until their brown scales split apart and a tiny, crumpled leaf pushed out into the light, as pale and soft as a baby's hand. Mina watched the green spread through the wood like a slow wave, beginning with the hawthorn at the edge of the clearing and ending, a few weeks later, with the great beeches at the top of the hill. It seemed to her that the whole forest was drawing one long, slow breath after the cold months of silence.

The days were longer and warmer now, and the forest floor, which had been brown and still all winter, was suddenly crowded with new life. A pale yellow butterfly rested on a primrose with its wings folded, and Tomas told her that it had spent the entire winter asleep as an adult, hidden among the ivy, waiting for exactly this kind of sun. Mina stood very still to see how long it would stay, and it stayed for a very long time.

Mina went straight to her marker stick, the first thing she did on the first warm morning, and knelt beside it with her heart beating faster than it ought. The acorn's shell had split from end to end, and out of the crack a pale, thick root had pushed itself into the soil, turning downward as determinedly as if it had known the way all along. She did not touch it, but she took a deep breath and let it out slowly.

Tomas explained that the root always emerges first, because a young plant must anchor itself and begin to find water before it does anything else. The two fat halves of the acorn stay in the soil and go on feeding the seedling from their store of food until it has leaves of its own with which to catch the sun. Mina thought that it was like leaving home with a packed lunch that has to last for weeks.

A root tip can sense which way is down, Tomas said, and bends to follow the pull of gravity, which is why a root grows downward even if the seed lies on its side. He suggested that Mina grow a bean in a glass jar on a damp paper towel at home and then turn the jar on its side, and she could watch the root change its mind within a day or two. She promised to try it that very evening, and went home with a bean already in her pocket.

Mina used a magnifying glass to study the tip of a weed's root that Tomas had pulled from the path, and she saw that it was covered in fine white hairs, thinner than any thread she owned. These root hairs, Tomas said, do most of the work of taking in water and dissolved minerals, and they live only for a short time, so that the root is always growing new ones just behind its tip. She imagined the acorn's root pushing through the dark, trailing its tiny hairs like a swimmer in cold water.

In the soil, a pale thread of fungus had found the tip of the young root and lay against it as lightly as a hair on a sleeve. Oak seedlings usually form their partnerships with fungi that are already waiting in the ground, Tomas said, and so Mina's acorn might soon have its very first partner, though he could not promise that it would be this particular fungus. She noted down the word maybe, and then crossed it out and wrote hopefully instead.

Mina laid a small ruler beside the acorn and measured the new root, which was about two centimetres long. She drew it in her notebook, with the shell split open above it like a pair of hands, and wrote the date beside it in her best handwriting. Her grandfather watched over her shoulder and told her that she was starting to sound, and look, like a real scientist.

Tomas took a stick and drew the roots of the oak in the dust, and Mina saw that they were not plunging straight down like a carrot, as she had expected, but spreading wide and shallow beneath the surface. They often reach farther than the branches do, he said, so that the hidden half of a tree can be as large as the half in the air. She looked from the drawing to the great trunk, trying to picture the hidden half.

Roots can sense where the soil is wetter, Tomas said, and they tend to grow in that direction, feeling their way along tiny differences in moisture much as a hand feels in the dark. When a root meets a stone, it does not stop but simply grows around it, like a river finding a way past a boulder. Mina thought that it was a remarkable kind of intelligence for something that has neither eyes nor brain.

Most of a tree's roots lie in the top layer of the soil, Tomas explained, because that is where the water, the air, the fallen leaves and the fungal partners are found, so a root seldom needs to dig deep. The finest, hair-thin roots of all spread through the upper soil like a net, and even a large oak may have few roots that go down more than a couple of metres. Mina was astonished to learn that the foundations of a giant could be so shallow.

Mina's seedling had begun life with a single long taproot, but the old oak looked quite different in Tomas's drawing, with a broad mat of roots across the ground and only a few thick ones that went deep. As an oak grows older, he said, it spreads sideways to gather more water and to hold itself up against the wind, and the first deep root becomes less important. Mina decided that this was like a child who leaves home and builds a whole village of friends.

Roots do two jobs at once, Tomas said, for they anchor the tree against the force of the wind and they bind the soil on hillsides, so that heavy rain cannot wash it down into the valley. The roots of neighbouring trees often weave together underground, which makes the whole wood stronger than any single tree could be, and a slope that has been stripped of trees can slide away in a storm. Mina looked at the mossy bank beside the path with new respect for the net of roots she could not see.

Mina stamped her foot on the path just to feel the ground, and Tomas gently asked her to step more softly. Roots need air as well as water, he explained, and soil that has been pressed hard by many boots, or by heavy machines, has less room for either, so that the roots beneath it struggle and grow poorly. She lifted her foot very carefully and promised herself that she would remember it every time she walked.

One morning Mina found a small green shoot rising out of the soil beside her faded marker stick, bent over like a hook as it pushed through the earth. As she watched, it straightened, shook off a crumb of soil, and opened its first tiny, deeply lobed leaves, which were unmistakably the leaves of an oak. She felt a thrill of recognition that was almost like meeting somebody she had been waiting for.

The seedling stood at the very edge of the old oak's shade, where the light was weak and the ground was crowded with its parent's roots. Oaks need plenty of light, Tomas said, and so a seedling that sprouts right under its parent has a very hard time of it, and most of those that try do not survive. He did not tell her that hers would die, but he did not tell her that it would live either, and she noticed, and was grateful for his honesty.

A deer had been browsing the young plants nearby, and several tiny seedlings had been bitten off at the ground, leaving only neat stumps. Mina's seedling had been spared, perhaps because a fern hid it, and Tomas reminded her that an oak makes many thousands of acorns in its life and needs only one of them to succeed. Luck, he said, is an important part of every forest, and so is the sheer number of chances that a tree provides.

Mina held a small ruler against the seedling, which stood about five centimetres tall, and counted its leaves, and wrote both numbers in her notebook. A seedling in the shade may wait for years for more light, Tomas told her, growing very slowly and storing up energy until a branch falls or a tree dies and the sunshine pours in. She knew that she would need to be patient, but she was beginning to think that patience might be a kind of skill, like drawing.

The great oak had opened its new leaves, and the whole tree was now a bright green cloud, so fresh that it seemed to hum in the sunlight. Each leaf was soft and pale and thin as paper at first, Tomas said, and hundreds of thousands of them would hang from a tree of this size before the summer was over. Mina found it difficult to imagine so much green growing from one small acorn.

Mina stood beneath the oak and tipped back her head, and the sunlight poured down through the leaves and dappled her face with moving gold. Every leaf is a miniature solar panel, Tomas said, because the chlorophyll in its cells captures the energy of the light and puts it to work making food. She held her hand up in the sun and tried to feel how much energy was falling on it.

Tomas drew arrows on a clean page of her notebook: light, water and a gas called carbon dioxide go into the leaf, sugar is made inside, and oxygen is released into the air. The whole process is called photosynthesis, he said, a word that means putting things together with light, and it is the basis of nearly all life on land. Mina looked at the arrows and thought that it was the simplest and the most important recipe in the world.

Tomas told her about a Flemish scientist named van Helmont, who lived about four hundred years ago and wondered where a tree gets the stuff to make its wood. He planted a little willow in a pot of carefully weighed soil, covered the soil, watered the tree with rainwater for five years, and then weighed everything again. Mina thought it must have been a very patient experiment, and Tomas agreed that it was one of the most famous in the history of science.

The willow had gained more than seventy kilograms, but the soil had lost less than sixty grams, and Van Helmont concluded that the tree must be made of the water he had given it. He was partly right, Tomas said, but he had missed something quite astonishing, which is that most of the new wood had been built from the air. Mina looked at the great oak and realised that it was largely made of a gas that she was breathing out.

A tree is built mostly from carbon, Tomas explained, and the carbon comes from the carbon dioxide in the air, which the leaves take in and join together into sugar and then into wood. About half of the dry weight of wood is carbon, so a trunk is, in a very real sense, air that has been turned into something solid. Mina laid her hand on the oak and thought that it was a very slow and very beautiful way of building a house.

As a tree makes sugar it releases oxygen, Tomas said, but trees are not the only source, and it is a mistake to call the forest the lungs of the world. Tiny algae in the oceans make a very large share of the oxygen in the air, and the forests, too, use a good deal of what they make, so the picture is less simple than the slogans suggest. Mina made a note to ask more careful questions whenever she heard a very neat claim.

The tree does not use all of its sugar for growth, Tomas said, because it also burns some of it to get energy, as an animal does, and it breathes out carbon dioxide as it does so, even at night. Some sugar is changed into starch and stored in the roots, ready to feed the buds and leaves when spring comes round again, so that the tree carries its own savings account. Mina thought of the roots under her feet as a pantry that was always full.

Mina studied the underside of a leaf through her magnifying glass and saw a fine pattern of veins like the lines of a road map. Scattered over the surface, Tomas told her, are tiny pores called stomata, far too small for her lens, and each is guarded by two cells that open or shut it as the leaf's water allows. When the pores are open, carbon dioxide enters but water vapour escapes, so every leaf lives in a constant balancing act between feeding itself and drying out.

On a hot, dry afternoon the leaves of the oak looked slightly limp, and Mina, who was sitting in the shade with a warm drink of water, felt rather limp herself. On days like this, Tomas said, a tree closes its stomata to save water, and so it takes in less carbon dioxide and makes less sugar, which is why a long drought can slow a tree's growth for years. She made a mental note that every living thing, from oaks to schoolgirls, has to work out how to cope with the heat.

Tomas pointed to the tall trunk and asked Mina how the water got from the roots to the highest leaves, and when she could not guess, he said that nobody could be blamed, for a tree has no heart. The answer, he promised, was far stranger than any pump, and he waited with great enjoyment for her to ask. Mina leaned against the oak and felt that something extraordinary was about to be explained.

The water that the roots take in climbs through narrow tubes of wood called xylem, and Tomas showed her a cut branch where a bundle of tiny openings looked like drinking straws. Most of the xylem is made of dead cells whose walls remain like the pipes of a ruined house, and yet it works perfectly well. Mina counted the little holes until she lost count, and decided that a tree is mostly plumbing.

Water evaporates from the surface of the leaves into the air, Tomas explained, and because water molecules cling to one another, each one that leaves tugs on the one behind it, drawing a continuous thread up from the roots. The tree does not push the water but pulls it, in the way that one drinks through a very long straw, and the sun does the work. Mina marvelled that such a simple idea could lift water to the top of the tallest tree.

The tallest trees in the world are more than a hundred metres high, and Tomas said that the water must travel all the way to their tops against the pull of gravity. Scientists have calculated that there may be a limit to how tall a tree can grow, somewhere around a hundred and twenty metres, because a thread of water that long becomes difficult to hold together. Mina tried to imagine a drink of water that had to travel the height of a tall building before it was allowed to be used.

Mina asked how much water a tree really uses, and Tomas answered that a large tree can lift hundreds of litres on a hot day, enough to fill a bathtub several times over. She tried to picture a line of buckets stretching away from the oak, each one full, and she realised that the tree was working hard even on the lazy afternoons when it seemed to be doing nothing at all. A forest, he added, is a great fountain that never splashes, and the oak was only one small jet of it.

Just beneath the bark, Tomas said, runs a second set of tubes called phloem, and Mina laid her palm against the trunk as though she could feel the flow. They carry sugar from the leaves to every part of the tree that needs energy, down to the roots and out to the growing tips and buds, and unlike the xylem they are made of living cells. She felt a rush of tenderness for the bark, which was guarding all this quiet traffic.

Tomas showed her a young tree with a ring of bark gnawed away around its trunk by deer or by voles, and the wood beneath it was pale and bare. Without the phloem, the sugar cannot travel to the roots, so a tree stripped all the way around will usually starve slowly from below and die, even though its leaves look healthy for a while. That, he said, was why foresters put guards around the trunks of young trees.

Mina noticed a crowd of tiny green aphids on the underside of a leaf, each one with its beak pushed into the phloem and drinking the sugary sap.
