They cannot use all of the sugar, Tomas said, and so they let fall small drops of sweet liquid, which ants collect with enthusiasm and which bees sometimes gather and turn into a dark, rich forest honey. She watched an ant stroke an aphid with its feelers, in a kind of ancient business deal.

Mina pressed her ear against the trunk of the oak and listened with her eyes closed, hoping to hear the water rushing upward, but all she heard was her own pulse. Scientists have recorded tiny clicks from trees in a drought, Tomas said, which they think are the sounds of the water columns breaking, but the sounds are far too faint and too high for people to hear without special instruments. She took her ear away, a little disappointed and a little thrilled, and decided to listen again on a hot day.

Tomas drew a loop in her notebook, with one arrow going up through the wood and another coming down through the bark, and Mina added the leaves, the roots and the word balance. Water rises in the xylem and sugar descends in the phloem, he said, so the whole tree is a living machine without a single moving part that anyone can see. She looked at the drawing, then at the oak, and for the first time the two matched exactly.

Mina woke before dawn to the loudest chorus of birdsong she had ever heard, and she crept out to the edge of the clearing with a blanket around her shoulders. A blue tit flew past her to a hole in a trunk, carrying a beakful of moss that stuck out on both sides like a fluffy moustache. Its mate was already inside, arranging the nest, and Mina watched with a smile.

A few weeks later, the same pair of blue tits was bringing food to a hole crowded with chicks, and the parents seemed never to stop for breath. The chicks need thousands of green caterpillars before they can leave the nest, Tomas said, so the whole family's timing is fixed to the opening of the oak leaves, when the caterpillars are most abundant. Mina counted twelve trips in ten minutes, and then she gave up, feeling quite exhausted on their behalf.

Tomas opened an old notebook of his own and showed her two lines that drew closer together year by year, one for the date on which the oak leaves opened and one for the date on which the caterpillars appeared. In very warm springs, he said, the leaves and the caterpillars can come earlier than the birds expect, and the chicks may hatch too late for the feast, so scientists watch this timing with real concern. Mina felt that she had been shown how fragile a clever arrangement can be.

The oak has flowers, although Mina had never seen them, and now Tomas showed her long yellow catkins hanging from the twigs like tassels, with tiny green female flowers sitting beside them. A single tree carries both kinds, he told her, and the wind carries the pollen from the hanging flowers to the female ones, often on a neighbouring tree. Mina stared at the nearly invisible flowers and understood that every acorn she had ever seen began as something so small.

Tomas tapped a pine branch with his stick, and a cloud of yellow dust rose into the sunshine and drifted away between the trunks like smoke. A tree that trusts the wind to carry its pollen must make millions upon millions of grains, he said, because almost all of them will never land on a flower. Mina sneezed, and he declared that this was exactly the proof he needed, since the pollen season had clearly begun.

On the willow catkins and the wild cherry blossom, the bees were working busily, their legs heavy with pollen and their bodies dusted with gold. Trees that depend on insects offer sweet nectar and bright flowers in exchange for being visited, and the bees, carrying pollen from blossom to blossom, quite unintentionally join separate trees together. Tomas said that early willow flowers are especially precious, because they feed the first bees at a time when almost nothing else is blooming.

Some years, Tomas told her, an oak makes an enormous crop of acorns, and other years almost none, and the forest floor beneath it looks quite different from one autumn to the next. Scientists are still debating exactly how oaks decide, and how neighbouring trees seem to agree, but it is thought that a huge crop in a single year means that the animals cannot possibly eat every acorn. Mina decided that this was a clever way of being generous without being ruined.

On the forest floor, bluebells and white wood anemones were in full bloom, spread in glowing carpets under the still-bare branches of the beeches. They hurry to flower, Tomas said, before the leaves overhead open and close out the light, and then they spend the rest of the year resting underground and storing up food for the next spring. Mina knelt among the flowers and thought that they must be among the busiest, and the briefest, residents of the wood.

On a low branch, a fluffy tawny owl chick was sitting with its eyes half closed, giving a thin, wheezing call that sounded rather like a rusty gate. Tomas whispered that young owls often leave the nest hole before they can fly well, and scramble about the branches while their parents bring food in the dark, so the chick was not lost and should be left alone. Mina looked up at the round hole she had noticed in the autumn and saw at once who had been living behind the door.

One golden evening Mina measured her seedling and found that it was about ten centimetres tall, with six small leaves that were beginning to darken from the pale green of the spring. The days were long now, and she stayed out until the light turned rose-coloured in the treetops and the first bats began to flicker above the clearing. Tomas, who had been waiting patiently with a flask of tea, said that she could stay as long as she wished.

A green caterpillar was chewing a lacy hole in a young oak leaf, and Mina watched it eat its way from the edge towards the middle with the steady rhythm of a tiny mower. The tree was not helpless, Tomas said, for an oak has several ways of defending itself, and the more Mina learned about them, the less she thought of the caterpillar as a harmless animal. She had never before looked closely at a leaf that was being eaten, and now she could not look away.

Something tickled Mina's neck, and when she brushed at it, she found a tiny caterpillar dangling from a silk thread, as neat as a spider on a line. Winter moth caterpillars lower themselves from the branches on silk, Tomas explained, and the breeze carries them to fresh leaves, so that on a still spring day the oak can seem to be raining caterpillars. Mina looked up into the leaves and saw a hundred threads shining in the sun.

In spring the oak leaves are soft, tender and rich in food, and the caterpillars devour them with enthusiasm, but as summer comes on, the leaves grow tougher and fill with bitter substances called tannins. Tannins make leaves hard to digest, Tomas said, and they are the same substances that people once used to turn animal skins into leather and that give strong tea its dry taste. Mina bit a corner of an old leaf and made such a face that he burst out laughing.

When a caterpillar bites into a leaf, the injury sets off an alarm inside the tree, and chemical messages travel along its vessels to other leaves. Some of those leaves begin making more of their bitter chemicals before the caterpillars reach them, Tomas said, so that a tree under attack soon becomes a less appetising meal. Mina thought that it was like a house in which the lights come on in every room as soon as someone opens the front door.

Mina tore a leaf in half and held it to her nose, and the smell that rose from it was so strong and so familiar that she laughed aloud, for it was exactly the smell of freshly cut grass. That scent, Tomas explained, is a mixture of chemicals that a damaged leaf releases into the air, and it is quite common among plants, whether in a meadow or in a wood. She tore another leaf, just to be sure, and the smell was the same.

In the 1980s, some scientists reported that trees growing near a damaged tree seemed to make more defensive chemicals themselves, as if they had smelled danger on the air. Other researchers found it hard to repeat those results, and later experiments with other plants have produced mixed answers, so scientists still debate how much it matters in a real forest. Tomas said that he found the uncertainty almost as interesting as the idea itself, and probably more honest.

A tiny wasp landed on the chewed leaf and crept along it, its antennae trembling, searching for the caterpillar. Some wasps lay their eggs inside caterpillars, Tomas said, and studies suggest that insect-eating birds are also attracted to trees that have been damaged by insects, perhaps because the smell tells them where to find a meal. Mina watched the wasp disappear around the edge of the leaf and wished it luck, though she was not sure which side she was on.

Mina wondered aloud whether the forest might be like a village, in which the trees warn each other of danger and join forces against their enemies, and she asked it very hopefully. Tomas said that it was a lovely picture, but that a tree does not make plans, because these responses were shaped by evolution over a very long time, and the trees that happened to respond well left more descendants. He added that the truth was less cosy than a village, and a good deal more extraordinary.

On a twig, Mina found a round brown ball about the size of a marble, and Tomas told her that it was called an oak apple, though it was not a fruit at all. A tiny gall wasp had laid an egg inside a bud, he said, and the tree had responded by growing a ball of tissue around it, which feeds and shelters the grub inside until it is ready to emerge. Mina turned the strange little ball over in her fingers and wondered who was inside.

People have used oak galls to make ink for many centuries, Tomas said, and many important old documents were written with it, long before anyone had heard of a ballpoint pen. He crushed a gall, mixed it with a little water and a pinch of iron salt, and handed Mina a feather, and she wrote her name on a scrap of paper in dark brown ink that slowly turned black. It struck her that the tree defended itself with a chemical that people had borrowed for their ideas.

By midsummer the fields beyond the trees were baking, but under the oak, beside the Stream, Mina and Tomas rested in a deep green room where the light was soft and the air felt like cool water. Tomas leaned back against the trunk with his hat over his eyes and said that this, in his opinion, was the best idea that trees had ever had. Mina took off her boots and let her feet hang above the water, feeling that the whole summer had stopped to rest.

Tomas had brought a small thermometer, and when he held it in the shade it read several degrees lower than it had in the open field. Trees cool the air in two ways, he explained: by blocking the sun with their leaves, and by releasing water vapour, which takes heat with it as it evaporates, in the same way that sweat cools skin. Mina held the thermometer up like a prize and declared that the forest had been air-conditioned by nature.

All the water that evaporates from the leaves ends up in the air, which is why a forest on a warm day feels fresh and damp, and why it smells of green things. Some scientists think that very large forests help to bring rain by sending so much vapour upward that it forms clouds, though the details are still being worked out and may depend on the place. Mina looked up at the narrow strip of sky between the leaves and imagined the invisible traffic of water moving through it.

A sudden shower swept over the wood, and Mina and Tomas stood beneath the thick canopy and found that they hardly got wet. The leaves caught the first drops, and the rest trickled down the branches and trunks, so that the water reached the soil slowly, which gave the ground time to soak it up instead of being swept away. Tomas said that a wooded hillside is a sponge, and Mina listened to the patter of the leaves with her eyes shut.

Mina lifted a flat stone from the bed of the Stream, and a few tiny creatures wriggled away from the sudden light, some of them in little cases made of sand and bits of stone. They were the young stages of mayflies and caddisflies, Tomas said, and they can live only in streams where the water is clean and cool, so that finding them is a kind of good report on the whole wood. She put the stone back exactly as she had found it, so that the little cases would not be disturbed.

Brown leaves from last autumn lay in the shallows, and a small grub was gnawing at the edge of one, leaving behind a lace of veins. Many of the creatures in a stream depend on the leaves that fall from the forest, Tomas said, so the food chain of the water begins in the trees, and a bare stream would have far less to eat. Mina saw that the boundary between the forest and the water was not a wall but a doorway.

A small brown bird, a dipper, bobbed on a wet stone, and then to Mina's delight it walked straight into the Stream and disappeared beneath the surface. The shade of the trees keeps the water cool, Tomas said, and cool water holds more oxygen, which trout and many other creatures need to breathe, so a stream with no trees beside it can become dangerously warm. Mina counted the seconds until the dipper reappeared, and it was a surprisingly long time.

As the sky turned pink, small dark shapes began to flicker over the clearing, swerving and diving with astonishing speed. They were bats, Tomas said, which sleep by day in cracks and holes in old trees, and a single bat can catch hundreds or even thousands of small insects in a night. Mina tried to follow one with her eyes, but it was gone before she had properly seen it, lost in the dusk.

At the edge of the forest Mina noticed tiny green lights glowing in the long grass, steady and pale, like stars that had fallen and could not get up. They were glow-worms, Tomas said, which are really beetles, and it is the wingless female that glows, to show the flying males where she is. Mina lay in the grass and watched them for a long time, and nobody spoke, because there was nothing at all to add.

Later, Mina and Tomas lay on a blanket and looked up at the stars scattered between the dark crowns of the trees, while an owl called somewhere far off. At night the oak stops making sugar, and Tomas said that scientists using lasers have measured the branches of some trees drooping a little in the dark, though nobody can say whether it is anything like sleep. Mina fell asleep wondering what a tree dreams about, if it dreams at all.

A summer storm broke without warning, and black clouds rolled over the treetops like a lid being closed on a pot. Mina and Tomas ran for a rocky overhang beside the path, and crouched beneath it while the first heavy drops struck the leaves and the whole forest began to roar. High above them, the crowns of the trees were thrashing and bending as if they were trying to take off.

Wind is good for trees, Tomas shouted above the noise, because a shaken tree grows a thicker, stronger trunk, while young trees held up by stakes in a nursery often grow thin and fall over when the stakes are removed. Mina watched the great oak sway in the gale and saw that its movement was not a sign of weakness but a kind of training. She thought that a tree that never felt the wind might be the weakest of all.

Mina noticed how different the trees looked in the field beside the wood, where a single oak had spread its branches wide in all directions like an enormous open umbrella. In the crowded forest, Tomas said, trees must race one another for light, so they grow tall and thin, with most of their branches high up, while a tree in the open can afford to grow broad and low. Mina imagined the same acorn growing into two very different trees, according to where it was planted.

A flash of lightning lit the whole forest in a single blue instant, and Mina clapped her hands over her ears before the thunder cracked right overhead. Tall trees are often struck, Tomas said, and some of them survive with a long scar that spirals down the trunk, while others lose their tops or are killed. Mina decided that the rocky overhang was an excellent place to be, and she moved a little closer to Tomas.

When the storm had passed, the forest dripped and steamed and smelled of wet earth, and Mina and Tomas walked out into the shining leaves. A little way off they found a giant beech lying on its side, and where its roots had been there stood a great vertical wall of earth and tangled roots, taller than Tomas, with stones still stuck in it. Mina stood in front of it with her mouth open, hardly able to believe that a living thing so big could be tipped over.

Mina reached out and touched the wall of roots, and found that it was wide but very thin, a flat plate of roots no deeper than her own arm. A beech spreads its roots close to the surface, Tomas explained, and after days of rain the soil had gone soft, so the wind pushing on the heavy, leafy crown levered the whole tree out of the ground. It was not a mistake, he said, but an ordinary event that forests have always survived.

A beam of sunlight fell through the hole in the canopy where the beech had stood, and it landed exactly beside Mina's marker stick, which she saw with a sudden leap of her heart. Her seedling was standing in direct light for the first time in its life, and the little leaves seemed to glow. She stared at it for a long moment with her hand pressed over her mouth, afraid that if she made a sound it might all disappear.

Tomas said that the gap would not stay empty for long, because the seeds in the soil and the seedlings waiting nearby would rush to take advantage of the light. Birch, rowan and bramble grow fast in full sun, while the oak and the beech that follow them grow more slowly and last longer, so a forest is really a patchwork of places of different ages. Mina looked at her small oak and realised that it was in a race, though not necessarily a hopeless one.

Near the Stream they came to an old pine with a long black scar running up one side of the trunk, and a few fresh green shoots sprouting from the bark near its base. A fire had gone through the wood a very long time ago, Tomas said, perhaps lit by lightning, and the pine had survived because its thick, corky bark protected its living layer from the heat. Mina laid her palm on the charred bark and felt how rough it was.

Tomas told her that in some pine forests the cones are sealed with resin and open only in the heat of a fire, releasing seeds onto bare, cleared ground where they have a good chance to grow. Fire is a natural part of some forests, he added, but today many fires burn much hotter and much more often than the trees can cope with, especially in droughts, and many of them are started by people. Mina looked at the old scar with new respect and a little fear, and she kept her hand on the bark.

Months later, the great beech was still lying where it had fallen, but it hardly looked like a tree any more, for moss and ferns had covered its bark and mushrooms stood in rows along its flanks like tiny lamps. Fungi, beetles and bacteria had already gone to work on the trunk, which would take years, even decades, to rot away completely. Mina climbed carefully onto the log and found it as springy as a mattress.

Mina peeled away a piece of soft, rotten wood and found a fat white grub curled inside it, as plump as a thumb. This was the young stage of a stag beetle, Tomas told her, and some beetle larvae spend several years inside a log before they finally emerge as adults, which makes a single fallen tree a long-term home. She put the wood back gently and thanked the grub, in a whisper, for letting her look.

Wood is hard to digest, Tomas explained, because it contains lignin, a tough substance that very few living things can break down, and the fungi that rot wood are among the most important of them. Without those fungi, fallen trunks would pile up for ever and the carbon and nutrients locked inside them would never return to the soil. Mina looked at the pale streaks in the log and saw them for the first time as the signs of an enormous, silent digestion.

All along the back of the log a row of tiny trees was growing in a neat line, as though someone had planted them with a ruler, and Mina knelt to count them. A rotting log is called a nurse log, Tomas said, because it holds water like a sponge, and the seedlings that sprout on top of it are lifted above the crowded forest floor and may find more light. In some wet forests, he added, you can find a row of mature trees standing on the stilt-like roots of a log that rotted away long ago.

As the log rots, the carbon stored in its wood is slowly released, much of it returning to the air as carbon dioxide, while some of it sinks into the soil and stays there for a long time. A fallen tree, Tomas said, is therefore like a bank account that is closed very gradually, paying out its wealth over decades. Mina thought that it was a strangely cheerful way of looking at a tree that had died.

Mina reached out to touch a pale mushroom that had pushed its way through the moss, and Tomas gently caught her hand. Some wild mushrooms are deadly poisonous, he told her, and a few of the most dangerous look almost exactly like harmless ones, so that nobody should ever eat one unless an expert has named it for certain. She nodded, looking at the beautiful, innocent-seeming thing, and was glad to have been stopped.

Tomas told her that one honey fungus in the state of Oregon, in the United States, has been found to cover about nine square kilometres, and that scientists think it may be thousands of years old. If the estimates are right, it is one of the largest living things on Earth, he said, though it lives almost entirely underground, and nobody sees it unless they know exactly where to look. Mina thought of the pale threads in the snow and tried to imagine them spreading across a whole valley.

Mina noticed that a cluster of honey-coloured mushrooms was growing around the base of a young tree that looked sickly, with thin leaves and a cracked trunk. Not all fungi are friends, Tomas said, and honey fungus is one of those that can attack living trees as well as dead ones, so that the same kind of living thread can nurture one tree and destroy another. Mina saw that the forest was not a friendly village after all but something older and more complicated.

Tomas told her about Dutch elm disease, which is caused by a fungus that is carried from tree to tree by bark beetles, and which killed many millions of elm trees across Europe and North America during the last century. In many towns, the great avenues of elms that had stood for generations were reduced to bare skeletons within a few years, and the loss changed the look of whole landscapes. Mina asked whether anything could have been done, and he said that scientists are still working on it.

Beside a bare ash tree, Mina sat on a log and wrote in her notebook while a thin fog drifted through the wood. Diseases can now travel the world with the trade in plants and timber, Tomas said, and ash trees across Europe are suffering from a fungus that arrived from Asia, though scientists are searching for trees that seem to resist it. At the bottom of the page Mina wrote one more sentence, which said that in a forest, death is never the end of the page.

On a rainy evening, Tomas took down a heavy book from the shelf, opened it on the kitchen table, and turned the pages until he found a photograph of a twisted pine clinging to a bare mountainside. It was one of the oldest living things on Earth, he said, and he wanted to tell her about it before summer was quite forgotten. Mina pulled her chair close, with a mug of hot chocolate in both hands.

The tree was a bristlecone pine, one of a group that grow high in the dry mountains of the western United States, and some of them are almost five thousand years old. That means that they were already growing when the pyramids of Egypt were built, Tomas said, and that they have lived through the whole of recorded history. Mina studied the photograph and tried to count the ages in her head, until she gave up and simply stared.

Bristlecone pines live so long because they grow very slowly in cold, dry places where few other living things can harm them, Tomas explained. Their wood is dense and full of resin, which resists rot and insects, and an old tree may keep only a thin strip of bark alive, and the rest of the trunk stands as bare wood polished by wind. Mina thought that a tree could be old not because it was lucky, but because it was careful.

Scientists have matched the rings of living bristlecones with those of old dead wood lying on the ground, Tomas said, and so built a record of years and weather that reaches back thousands of years. Each ring is a year, each year was a different kind of weather, and together they make one of the longest diaries that nature has ever kept. Mina remembered the stump on the path and her sixty-one rings, and smiled at how small they seemed.

Tomas turned the page and showed her a photograph of the coast redwoods, which grow along the foggy Pacific coast of California and whose tops vanish into the mist. They are the tallest trees in the world, he said, and the tallest of them are well over a hundred metres high, taller than the Statue of Liberty, and one has even had a tunnel cut through its trunk. Mina held the picture close to her face, as though she might step into it.

Redwood roots are surprisingly shallow, Tomas said, but they spread wide and join the roots of neighbouring trees, so that the whole grove helps to hold itself up, and each tree leans on the others. High in the crowns of the oldest redwoods there are even patches of soil in the forks of the branches, and small animals live up there, never touching the ground. Mina thought of an entire town in the sky, and wondered what its children were called.

Autumn had come around again, and the oak was dropping its leaves exactly as it had a year before, though now Mina could name almost everything that was happening inside it. Mina and Tomas walked through the falling gold leaves along the same path they had taken on the first morning, and he let her lead the way, as he had begun to do some weeks before without saying so. She no longer saw a crowd of separate trees, but a slow, tangled community.

Mina hurried to the spot where the stick stood, faded now to a pale grey, and knelt in the grass with her heart in her mouth. There, beside it, stood her seedling, upright and green and a year older, with a bud already formed for the spring, and she let out a long breath that she seemed to have been holding since the summer. Tomas, behind her, said nothing, but she could hear from his breathing that he was smiling.

The little oak was still very small, hardly taller than her hand, but the gap left by the fallen beech had given it far more light than most seedlings ever get. It had survived frost, hungry animals and the deep shade, Tomas reminded her, and most acorns never get this far, but it might take many years to reach the canopy, and it would need patience. Mina measured it against her palm and, although it was little bigger than her hand, she felt unreasonably proud.

Tomas placed three seeds on Mina's palm: a tiny redwood seed, a bristlecone seed and an acorn, and the first two were so small that she could hardly see them. Every giant in the world began like this, he said, from a seed that could sit in a child's hand, and what makes it a giant is time, light, water, luck and a great many partners that nobody ever sees. Mina closed her fingers around the seeds and understood that her oak was only at the very beginning of a story.

Mina pressed both hands against the trunk of the oak and felt the sunlight warming the leaves high above her, and Tomas said that this warmth was being turned, quietly, into something that lasts. As trees grow, they draw carbon dioxide out of the air and lock the carbon into their trunks, branches, roots and the soil around them, and so a forest is a great storehouse of carbon. She had thought of the oak as a beautiful thing, but she now saw that it was also a working part of the world.

Forests act as stores of carbon, Tomas said, and when they are burned, cleared or left to dry out, some of it returns to the air as the same gas that is warming the planet. Keeping old forests standing is therefore among the most useful things that people can do, he added quietly, although it cannot replace cutting pollution, and it would be wrong to pretend that trees alone can do the whole job. Mina nodded slowly, determined never to promise more than the facts allowed, and wrote the words not alone in her notebook.

Mina had come to see that a forest is far more than a crowd of trees, for it shelters countless animals, holds the soil in place with its roots and helps to keep streams clear and clean. Rain that falls on a wooded slope is slowed by the leaves and soaked up by the soil, Tomas said, rather than rushing away all at once. She watched a deer lower its head to drink at the Stream, and tried not to move.

Tomas told her that planting trees is a fine thing to do, provided that the right kinds are planted in the right places and are looked after for years afterwards. Not every open place should become a wood, he warned, because some grasslands, meadows and bogs are precious habitats in their own right, and a tree planted in the wrong place can do more harm than good. Mina wrote the words right place in her notebook and underlined them twice, to be sure.

Protecting the forests that already exist matters just as much, Tomas said, because an old forest holds soil, fungal threads and ancient trees that no planting can replace in a lifetime. Mina thought of the pale threads she had seen in the snow and the hub trees that scientists were still studying, and she understood that some things in a forest are built too slowly to be rebuilt. He said that every wood, however small, is worth a defender, and that she could begin with the one at the end of her own street.

On a bright morning in the village, Mina and her neighbours gathered in a sunny field to plant a young tree that Tomas had chosen with the greatest care. Mina dug the hole with a borrowed spade, set the roots gently in the ground, and pressed the soil down around them, and when she stood up, her hands were dirty and her face was shining. It would be many years before the little tree gave any shade, but for now it stood in the field like a promise.

Before they turned for home on their last walk, Tomas gave her two rules that a forester learns early: leave deadwood where it lies, and walk lightly. Deadwood feeds countless creatures and fungi, he explained, and soil that is crushed by many boots becomes hard for roots to grow in, so both rules were really about respect. They were small rules, he admitted, and Mina said them aloud twice, as though learning a spell.

That evening, Mina sat by the window with a candle and read her whole notebook from the first page, and she smiled at the very first line, which said only one acorn. Her three columns had changed over the year, for many things that had been unknown in the beginning were now known to her, and the unknown column was still the longest, but its questions were better. She turned back to the question mark on the first page and decided that it was still the most important mark in the book.

The next morning, Mina walked alone along the path where her year had begun, with the leaves rustling around her boots and the sun low and golden through the trunks. Under the oak lay hundreds of acorns, most of which would become food, and she searched among them until she found one that was sound and smooth and heavy for its size, with its cap still fitting neatly. She held it up to the light and imagined the tiny tree folded inside.

Mina chose a sound acorn from the path, pressed it into the soft earth at the edge of the wood, and pushed a new stick in beside it, just as she had done a year before. She would be old before it stood as high as the great oak, and perhaps this seed would never make it at all, yet she felt as if she had joined something far larger than herself. Tomas put a hand on her shoulder, and above them the forest went quietly on growing.
